Push versus pull is the question of whether anything in nature ever pulls . Every textbook force can attract: gravitation attracts always, electrostatic and magnetic forces attract in half of their cases, and the nuclear forces bind. A tradition that runs through this collection from Newton to the present holds that not one of these is really a pull — that a body cannot reach across a gap and draw another towards it, and that wherever attraction is observed something is arriving from outside and pushing .
The claim is not that the equations are wrong. Almost everyone making it keeps Coulomb's law and the inverse square. The claim is about what the equations describe: whether the minus sign in front of an attractive potential names a real tug, or bookkeeping for an imbalance in a pressure that is doing all the work.
The standard account
Modern physics recognises four interactions and has no objection in principle to any of them attracting. A force is derived from a potential, and the direction in which a body moves is decided by the sign of the potential's gradient; nothing in the formalism prefers repulsion. In quantum field theory the interaction is carried by exchange, and attraction between unlike charges is as ordinary a result as repulsion between like ones. In general relativity gravity is not a force at all: bodies follow geodesics of a geometry shaped by mass-energy, so the question of what pulls does not arise.
The mainstream position on the old objection — that attraction requires action at a distance — is that field theory answered it in the nineteenth century. The field is local, it carries energy and momentum of its own, and each body responds to the field where it is. Nothing crosses empty space instantaneously, and nothing reaches.

Quasars (quasi-stellar objects, or QSOs) are compact, extremely luminous objects with very large redshifts . They are the single most contested class of object in modern cosmology, and the principal battleground between standard cosmology and the critical tradition documented on this wiki.
Mainstream astronomy reads a quasar's large redshift as purely cosmological, and therefore places quasars at the greatest distances in the observable universe — making them the most luminous objects known. A substantial body of observational work, led above all by the astronomer Halton C Arp , contends that this interpretation is mistaken: that quasars are far nearer than assumed , that much of their redshift is intrinsic rather than cosmological, and that they are ejected from the nuclei of active nearby galaxies . If so, the redshift–distance relation fails precisely where cosmology most depends on it, and the Big Bang distance scale must be rebuilt.
The standard picture
On the conventional account a quasar is the nucleus of a young, distant galaxy powered by matter accreting onto a supermassive black hole. Its redshift is taken to arise wholly from cosmic expansion, placing typical quasars billions of light-years away, and requiring luminosities hundreds of times that of an entire galaxy. This is the interpretation found in textbooks and assumed by most survey work.

Discordant associations and ejection

Abstract
The "Big Bang" model has ascended to a powerful position in modern cosmology over the past few decades. This position has become so strong that investigation of alternate ideas has almost ceased. Observational counter-evidence certainly exists (for reviews see e.g. Arp 1987; Sulentic 1987; Tifft 1987). The general belief is that this counter-evidence consists of misinterpreted data and false clues. One could easily get the impression that all of the observations fit easily into the accepted model. In fact, at least three new concepts have assumed great importance in preserving the Big Bang against observational and theoretical challenges. In temporal order of acclamation they are: 1) black holes; 2) merger phenomena and 3) dark matter. Gravitational accretiion onto supermassive black holes was required as soon as it became generally accepted that the quasar redshifts were cosmological (i.e. proportional to their distance). It provides a mechanism for producing the enormous energies implied by the assumption that quasars are at their redshift distances. Mergers came upon the scene in order to account for nearby peculiar galaxies and for the increasing luminosity and size of many objects at higher redshift. Dark matter helps to bind the groups and clusters of galaxies as well as to explain the flat rotation curves in spirals. In reality, it can help to fit almost any observation into the conventional picture. What is the observational evidence for the above three phenomena?

title: Questioning the Cosmological Doppler Red-Shift

Title Questioning the Cosmological Doppler Red-Shift
Read in full Link to paper
Author(s) Raymond H Gallucci
Keywords Tired Light , Universe Expansion, Doppler Shift
Published 2015
No. of pages 3
Abstract
Linked with the concept of a cosmological Doppler red-shift is an expanding universe with rapidly receding stars, galaxies, etc. Assuming no form of matter, especially a reasonably macroscopic and tenuous one like a star, let alone an entire galaxy, could possibly travel at speeds approaching that of light and remain ‘intact’ (except, perhaps, something as dense as a neutron star), the only possible way for such an entity to exhibit recession speeds approaching that of light would be for space itself to be expanding. And whether one accepts the traditional or Galilean Doppler red-shift as the correct explanation, one is still left to conclude that ‘something’ is ‘racing away.’ I endeavor to cast doubt on the traditional explanation of a cosmological Doppler red-shift due to universe expansion. A Galilean Doppler red-shift may be an equally plausible explanation for those who adhere to the premise of stars, galaxies, etc., receding for whatever reason.

Abstract
The "Electric Universe" Theory (EUT) owes part of its inspiration to the work of Immanuel Velikovsky ( Worlds in Collision [1950]), at least for introducing the concept of catastrophism of an electrical nature potentially inducing what EUT proponents see as plasma-arced "scarring" on some planets and other objects within our solar system, such as Mars. Though discredited by mainstream physicists and astronomers since the publication of his ideas in 1950, Velikovsky nonetheless ushered in an era where catastrophic events, rather than just immeasurable eons of uniformitarianism, became acknowledged as a potential contributor to the current state of our solar system (and maybe beyond). Based on my admittedly quite crude calculations in this paper, it still appears too far-fetched to believe the planet Venus arose out of Jupiter and careened through the inner solar system anytime within human history (if ever at all). However, this does not invalidate the EUT contention that planetary scarring due to electrical plasma-arcing may be responsible for the bizarre surface features seen on Mars and perhaps other celestial objects. But just what particular planetoids or comets might have been responsible for this remains unknown.

Ralph E. Juergens (6 May 1924 – 2 November 1979) was an American civil engineer and technical editor, remembered for two things: his part in documenting the scientific establishment's treatment of Immanuel Velikovsky , and his proposal that the Sun is powered electrically rather than by nuclear fusion.
The second is the more consequential. In 1972 he argued that the Sun is not a self-contained thermonuclear furnace but the focus of a cosmic electric discharge, drawing its radiant energy from the galaxy around it. Astrophysics does not accept the idea, but it became the founding statement of the electric Sun model and, through that, of the electric universe literature; Wallace Thornhill has written that the electric universe model "follows the brilliant work of Ralph Juergens".
Velikovsky himself never accepted it. The thermonuclear account of the Sun seemed sound to him, and he declined to follow the man who had done more than almost anyone to defend him.

He was Associate Editor of Pensée and a Senior Editor of Kronos , the two journals in which most of his writing appeared.

Ralph G. Beil (born 1938) is an American mathematical physicist. Over some two decades he developed a programme that uses Finsler geometry to construct a unified field theory, deriving electromagnetism and other interactions from the geometry of the tangent bundle. The Beil metric , a Finsler metric he introduced for this purpose, is named after him and has been taken up by later workers in the field.
Scientific work
Beil's work belongs to the tradition, going back to Weyl, Kaluza and Klein, of seeking to unify the forces of physics within an enlarged geometry. His distinctive move was to base that geometry not on ordinary Riemannian spacetime but on Finsler geometry — a generalization in which the metric can depend on direction as well as position — and to build it on the tangent bundle of spacetime.
In a sequence of papers beginning in the late 1980s he argued that a physical motivation for Finsler structure can be developed through gauge transformations on the tangent space, producing a correspondence in which geometric objects — metrics, connections and curvatures — play the roles of the physical gauge potentials, fields and energy-momentum. From this he recovered electrodynamics "from a metric," treated the classical charged particle as an extended geometric object, and extended the scheme toward the electroweak interaction with his work on "electroweak symmetry on the tangent bundle." The Beil metric introduced in this programme has since been studied by other geometers as a basis for unified field theories. Beil presented the approach at the 1995 Joint Summer Research Conference on Finsler Geometry, published in the American Mathematical Society volume Finsler Geometry (1996).

Nuclear electric dipoles
Sansbury's central proposal is that an atomic nucleus is not an inert charge but contains a small orbital component — he estimates its mass at around 10 −55 kg — which can be displaced by an applied electric force to leave the nucleus polarised. Because ordinary matter's outer electrons screen static fields, he argues that polarisation survives only where the applied force is changing, which he takes to be the general case in rotating and orbiting bodies.
His experimental contribution is a 1985 paper in the Review of Scientific Instruments reporting a force between a charged metal foil and a current-carrying conductor — an effect not predicted by standard electrodynamics, since a neutral current-carrying wire should exert no net electrostatic force. Claims of this general kind have a small literature; the best known, by Edwards and collaborators in 1976, was not confirmed by later searches.

Redshift is the observed shift of spectral lines from distant astronomical objects toward longer (redder) wavelengths, conventionally denoted z . It is the single most consequential measurement in modern cosmology: the entire extragalactic distance scale, the expansion of the universe, and the Big Bang itself all rest on one particular interpretation of what redshift means.
That interpretation — that redshift is essentially a velocity effect, so that a larger redshift means a greater distance and a faster recession — is precisely what the critical tradition documented on this wiki disputes. The observation itself is not in question; the inference from it is. A substantial body of work catalogued here argues that redshift can be produced by several physical processes that have nothing to do with recession, that some redshift is intrinsic to the object, and that in consequence redshift is not a reliable measure of distance — which would remove the observational foundation of the expanding-universe model.
The observation
When light from a distant source is dispersed into a spectrum, the characteristic absorption and emission lines of known elements appear at longer wavelengths than they do in the laboratory. The fractional shift, z = Δλ⁄λ, is straightforward to measure and is not itself controversial. Everything that follows depends on what is held to cause it.

Year 1976 onward
Redshift quantization , also called redshift periodicity , is the claim that the redshifts of galaxies and quasars are not distributed smoothly but cluster around preferred, regularly spaced values . If the claim holds, it is difficult to reconcile with redshift as a simple measure of recession velocity, since a genuine distribution of velocities and distances should be continuous. It is therefore among the strongest observational arguments for an intrinsic , non-velocity component in redshift, and against the Big Bang interpretation of the redshift–distance relation.
The observational claim
The effect was first reported by the astronomer William G Tifft of the University of Arizona in the 1970s, who found that galaxy redshifts appeared to fall into steps rather than a continuum. Subsequent work identified periodicities of roughly 72 km/s and various submultiples.
The most careful confirmations came from Bruce Guthrie and William Napier, who in 1990 reported a periodicity of similar magnitude in a sample restricted to bright spiral galaxies. Their final analysis concluded that extragalactic redshifts are quantized in the galactocentric frame of reference — that is, after correcting for the Sun's motion within our own galaxy — with periodicities of about 37.5 km/s among field galaxies and loose groups, and about 71.1 km/s in dense cluster environments. They argued the result could not be attributed to statistical artefacts, selection procedures, or flawed reduction techniques.

filename: Reference-Frame Independent Dynamics, Or How to Get Off Einstein's Train.html
title: Reference-Frame Independent Dynamics, Or How to Get Off Einstein's Train
content_preview:
Title Reference-Frame Independent Dynamics, Or How to Get Off Einstein's Train
Read in full Link to paper
Author(s) Greg Volk
Keywords Hertzian Electromagnetism, convective derivative, reference frame, Mach's Principle, universal instant, Maxwell's equations
Published 2009
No. of pages 12
Abstract
Einstein spent his life trying to develop a system of dynamics independent of reference frame. But this lofty goal demands a hard look at the very meaning of reference frame, a starting point for this paper. Einstein's fruitless attempts were based on his own observer-based theory of relativity, in turn based on Lorentzian covariant paradigms. Covariant mathematics admits transformations between coordinate systems and reference frames, but does not suggest a path towards invariance. However, the del operator provides a means of expressing spatial derivatives independent of coordinate system. Likewise, if time is independent of space, as this paper suggests, the total time derivative operator, d/dt, is also independent of reference frame. Therefore, physical equations that can be expressed with the del operator and the total time derivative, as opposed to reference-frame dependent partial derivatives, are naturally independent of reference frame. In particular, Maxwell's equations can be correct only if expressible by the del and d/dt operators, as proposed by Hertz and more recently advocated by Phipps. From fluid dynamics, developed by Bernoulli, Euler, Langrange, and many others, over a hundred years before Maxwell, we have the convective or Lagrangian time derivative d/dt = d/dt + v • del. Both sides of this equality are independent of observer, but the two right-hand terms differ in weight depending on how an observer moves with respect to the quantity being differentiated. One observer might see a buildup of material, while another sees an altered flow; one observer might see a changing field, another an acceleration. But the total change, the sum, remains invariant.

Reginald Irvan Gray , O.B.E. He is best remembered among independent-science circles for his lifelong study of classical electromagnetism in the tradition of James Clerk Maxwell , for a series of experiments probing fundamental questions such as the finite mass of the photon and the possible presence of neutrinos in the vacuum, and for his book Unified Physics (1988).
Biography
Gray served during the Second World War as a Group Captain in the Royal Air Force and was appointed an Officer of the Order of the British Empire ( O.B.E. ). He was counted among "the few," the RAF airmen of the wartime generation, and by contemporaries was described as an exceptionally modest man who seldom spoke of his wartime service.
After the war Gray emigrated to the United States, where he was employed as a physicist at a U.S. Navy laboratory. He became known within the community of independent physicists from the late 1960s onward, carrying out carefully crafted experiments—initially on his own initiative and later with some support from his laboratory. He settled in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, and continued both experimental and theoretical work through his years of retirement until his death in 1996.
Scientific contributions
Gray's work centred on classical electromagnetic theory and its experimental application. Title Reproducing the Pioneer 10 Anomaly with a Cosmic Lens

Abstract
Anderson et al. say: ?We have reported an anomalous, constant acceleration of Pioneer 10 and 11, a = (8.74 "1.33)E-8 cm/s 2 , directed towards the Sun, at distances ~20 - 70 AU." This anomaly can be reproduced by a multi-layer, onion-like, spherical cosmic lens centered on the Sun with an inner radius of 20 AU. If the effect stops at around 70 AU then the lens has eight layers, and the outer radius of the lens is 68.58 AU, and the effective refraction index through the eight layers is 1.000587235. If the effect extends beyond 70 AU, then there are more than eight layers. The innermost layer has a thickness of 3.33 AU and a refraction index of 1.000067963, and the eighth layer has a thickness of 9.79 AU and a refraction index of 1.000155628. The ratios between the volumes of adjacent lens layers is a constant, and that constant is within 0.2% of 4 1/3 . In order to make the volume ratios exactly equal to 4 1/3 , the anomaly error bars need to change from ?1.3300 to ?1.3357. The anomalous acceleration towards the Sun is just the calculated "observed" acceleration minus the Newtonian acceleration. The Newtonian acceleration is simply a = GM/R 2 , where GM is the heliocentric gravitation constant, and R is the radial distance from the Sun to the spacecraft. The calculated "observed" acceleration is just the Newtonian acceleration times the effective index of refraction at the spacecraft's location. The effective index of refraction is the product of the individual layer refraction indexes that are interior to the spacecraft's location.

Abstract
Doppler shift observations of spacecraft, such as Galileo, NEAR, Cassini, Rosetta and MESSENGER in earth flybys, have all revealed unexplained speed "anomalies" - that the Doppler-shift determined speeds are inconsistent with expected speeds. Here it is shown that these speed anomalies are not real and are actually the result of using an incorrect relationship between the observed Doppler shift and the speed of the spacecraft - a relationship based on the assumption that the speed of light is isotropic in all frames, viz invariant. Taking account of the repeatedly measured light-speed anisotropy the anomalies are resolved ab initio. The Pioneer 10/11 anomalies are discussed, but not resolved. The spacecraft observations demonstrate again that the speed of light is not invariant, and is isotropic only with respect to a dynamical 3-space. The existing Doppler shift data also o ers a resource to characterise a new form of gravitational waves, the dynamical 3-space turbulence, that has also been detected by other techniques. The Einstein spacetime formalism uses a special definition of space and time coordinates that mandates light speed invariance for all observers, but which is easily misunderstood and misapplied.

Abstract
Cosmology, in its broadest sense, may be defined as the study of the universe in terms of its origin, its fundamental makeup, and its development in time. Many theories of cosmology have been proposed, and each assumes one or more models by which various phenomena, which are sensed by man or his instruments, are explained. Most of these theories and models are incomplete and thus leave room for alternate theories and explanations. Rhysmonic cosmology is a "new" theory which starts from fundamental premises and therefore builds-up a model of the universe from a firm foundation. It is the aim of this monograph to introduce the reader to these new concepts and to lead the reader in the development of this cosmology in a logical manner. The theory will not only explain much of what is assumed to be known of this universe, but will also develop new knowledge which will lead to testable predictions and perhaps new and fascinating technologies. The theory also provides logical explanations for many present day enigmas, especially those of an astronomical nature. While the author recognizes that this material is yet incomplete, sufficient information and data will be provided to enable many other independent investigations into this new cosmology. On this wiki he appears chiefly as the author of arguments that contributors here dispute, and as the physicist whose own doubts about renormalization are most often quoted back at the theory.
Feynman worked on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos, taught at Cornell from 1945 and at Caltech from 1950. Between 1947 and 1949 he, Julian Schwinger and Sin-Itiro Tomonaga independently produced formulations of quantum electrodynamics in which the divergent integrals of the theory are absorbed into redefinitions of the measured mass and charge of the electron; Freeman Dyson showed the three formulations to be equivalent, and the three shared the 1965 Nobel Prize. Feynman's route ran through his path-integral formulation of quantum mechanics, in which an amplitude is computed by summing a phase over every possible history, and through the diagrams that encode the terms of the perturbation expansion.

Robert E. Var is an American independent theoretical physicist based in Waltham, Massachusetts. Over nearly three decades he developed a programme — beginning with "space-energy theory" and culminating in "hyper-energy theory" — that treats space as a physical, energy-dense medium and seeks to derive gravity, relativity and cosmology from its dynamics.
Scientific work
Var's central idea is that space is not empty but a medium carrying an enormous intrinsic energy density, and that gravity is a local reduction of that density caused by mass — a principle he attributes to a gravitation theorem published by Maxwell in 1864. His first statement of the approach, " On a New Mathematical Framework for Fundamental Theoretical Physics ," appeared in the mainstream journal Foundations of Physics in 1975.
He later expanded it into a hierarchy of gauge-field theories: a velocity-dependent formulation he argues reproduces special relativity , a tensor "Einstein–Maxwell" theory he offers as a quantizable account of gravity, and finally hyper-energy theory , a many-dimensional cosmology in which the universe is a compressible medium of mass-energy with extra compactified dimensions sourced by the flow of time. He presents this framework as accounting for the big bang , cosmic inflation, the elementary-particle spectrum, and the physical nature of time and superstrings. This later work is largely unpublished and lies outside the scientific mainstream.

The Rodin coil is a toroidal winding pattern devised by Marko Rodin , in which the conductor is wound around a torus in a repeating star-like sequence rather than in the usual evenly spaced circular loops. It is one of the most widely replicated devices in the amateur new energy community, and a substantial body of experimental reports on it is catalogued on this wiki.
The winding
A conventional toroidal coil is wound so that successive turns lie side by side around the ring. In the Rodin pattern the winding instead skips a fixed number of positions on each pass, so that the conductor traces a closed star polygon over the surface of the torus and returns to its starting point only after several circuits. The result is that the current paths cross one another at intervals and the turns are not parallel, which is the feature its advocates regard as essential.
Rodin derived the sequence from what he calls vortex-based mathematics , a scheme built on the repeating digit-sum patterns that appear when the numbers 1–9 are doubled repeatedly (1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 5 and back to 1, with 3, 6 and 9 standing apart). He describes the winding as following "the longest free-flowing path of the electron", and identifies the 3–6–9 triad as governing a flux perpendicular to the coil surface.
Claims
Rodin and those following him have attributed a wide range of properties to the coil, including:
an unusually strong and well-collimated magnetic field along the torus axis, described as a toroidal pinch ;
applications to fusion confinement, brushless motors, high-sensitivity antennas and propulsion;
in the stronger versions of the claim, gravitational effects and energy gain.

In March 1989, Roger Stringham of First Gate Energies, in Hawaii, USA pioneered the method of using acoustic cavitation to produce the cold fusion effect. Acoustic cavitation uses ultrasonic waves to create gas bubbles within the heavy water. Stringham was the first to use the term "sonofusion" to describe how this phenomenon creates energy in cold fusion experiments.
This work is not be confused with other experiments in the hot fusion field which also use a form of acoustic cavitation, called "acoustic inertial confinement fusion." The two types of research are markedly different.
The key differences with the cold fusion method, sonofusion, is that the effect is directly related to an as-yet-unknown interaction between heavy water and a host metal, such as palladium. The hot fusion method does not employ a host metal. The other key distinction between the cold fusion and hot fusion method is that the cold fusion method produces no deadly neutron radiation, as occurs in hot fusion. -- Steven B. Krivit https://web.archive.org/web/20150425151413/http://newenergytimes.com/v2/views/StringhamR/StringhamR.shtml

Roland H. Dishington (1919 – 15 January 2016) was an American physicist who spent much of his career in the aerospace industry at TRW , and who developed over several decades an independent programme in which matter, charge and energy are all distributions and distortions of a single aether .
His work is unusually coherent for an independent programme: a small number of commitments, applied consistently across electromagnetism, particle structure and the conservation laws, and set out across four books and a series of papers. He argued the case in the technical language of classical field theory rather than by analogy, and his most-read paper is addressed directly to what he considered errors in the standard textbooks .
The aether as the one substance
Dishington's starting point is that space and matter are not two things. In The Extended Electron he describes matter and space as disproportionate distributions of the aether — the same substance, differently concentrated — and in Energy and Charge he accounts for energy and charge as distortions of that substance.
His stated method is worth recording, because it explains the shape of everything he wrote:
If there is no picture to illustrate a theory, constructing one and backing it up with a strong, simple-as-possible mathematical representation is the way to get to new technologies in the shortest time.
— Roland H. Dishington, The Extended Electron
That is the demand for intelligibility that runs through most of the work catalogued on this wiki — a theory should admit of a picture, and the mathematics should represent the picture rather than replace it. See Aether .

Title Rotating Mossbauer Experiments and the Speed of Light

Volume 3

Abstract
Champeney's 1963 Mossbauer experiment was performed as a first-order test of "ether" velocity, in spite of an earlier paper that proved that there was exact cancellation between two first-order effects, one due to "ether" velocity, and the other due to Lorentz "time" dilation. But experiments show that clock rates are determined by their velocity with respect to non-rating geocentric coordinates. The first-order term "time dilation" term thus reappears, which must be balanced by another, if agreement with the experiment is to be achieved.

Russ Gries is an independent experimental researcher who runs RWGresearch , an open-source "garage lab" project that attempts to build and test claimed new-energy, plasma, cold fusion/LENR and Tesla -related devices, and publishes the attempts as they happen through his YouTube channel and the open-source-energy.org forum. He is best known within the independent-inventor community not for a theory of his own but for a working method: rather than asserting that a claimed effect is real, he builds the device, instruments it, and shows the result — whatever the result is — to an audience that is invited to criticise it.
Biography
Published sources say little about Gries's personal background, and this article does not speculate about it. What is documented is his research practice. RWGresearch was created, in his own description, "to help Russ promote his work, share his results and work as a team with his subscribers", and it operates as a small home laboratory funded by viewer donations and built largely from salvaged parts. He has emphasised that serious experimental work does not require an institutional budget, noting for example that "old CRT TVs and computer monitors people are throwing out every day have a lot of good magnet wire in them", and that most of his early coils were wound from recycled material at essentially no cost.
He maintains the RWGresearch website and forum presence, broadcasts live experimental sessions, and for several years ran an annual community "Pulse Motor Build-Off" (documented from 2012 to 2020) in which participants built and compared competing motor designs.

Title SN 1987A and the Neutrino

Published Society for the Advancement of Autodynamics

"SN 1987A and the Neutrino" is a paper by Ricardo L Carezani challenging the neutrino detections associated with the supernova of February 1987 in the Large Magellanic Cloud — the observation generally regarded as the founding event of neutrino astronomy. Carezani sets out seven numbered "facts" against it.
Overview
Carezani begins from a published summary of the evidence: "The coincidence between the two results provides OVERWHELMING evidence that the neutrinos, formed at the instant the supernova's core collapsed, did INDEED come from this star". His objection is first to the form of the argument — "We suppose what we are trying to prove: neutrinos!" — and then to the data behind it.
The argument
The seven facts
Fact 1. Of four detectors then operating, one — Mont Blanc — recorded the first claimed burst, at 02:52:36.8 UT. IMB, Kamiokande II and the South Dakota experiment did not. Twenty-five per cent agreement, Carezani argues, is not overwhelming evidence.
Fact 2. Even granting simultaneity between Mont Blanc and Kamiokande II, two of four detectors saw nothing, so the agreement is at best 50 per cent.
Fact 3. Producing the assumed flux from 180,000 light years away requires converting 10 to 15 per cent of a solar mass to neutrinos. No mechanism for this is supplied, and the mechanism would differ from anything known in stars.
Fact 4. To explain neutrinos arriving at Kamiokande II twelve seconds after the first burst, a "neutrino sphere" some tens of kilometres in radius is invoked to trap and release them. Title Sagnac and Gravitation
Author(s) Petr Beckmann
Keywords Sagnac effect , gravitation, non-Euclidean geometry, ether
Published 1992
Volume 3
Number 1
Pages 9-12
Abstract
The Einstein theory is sometimes incorrectly accused of being unable to explain the Sagnac effect (even for an unclosed path configuration). However, its explanation reveals that it works with the gravitational field as the equivalent of an ether, in which the velocity of light is not constant unless space is distorted into a non-Euclidean geometry so as to force its constancy. Although not wrong in the sense of disagreeing with experimental results, this mathematical formalism is complicated, opaque and unnecessary, for it is easily replaced by very simple mathematics in Euclidean space yielding the same result when it is assumed that the velocity of light is constant with respect to the local gravitational field; this requires no special non-Euclidean space.

filename: Satellite Motion in a Non-Singular Gravitational Potential.html
title: Satellite Motion in a Non-Singular Gravitational Potential
content_preview:
Title Satellite Motion in a Non-Singular Gravitational Potential
Author(s) Ioannis Iraklis Haranas , Spiros Pagiatakis
Keywords Non-singular potential, Lagrange planetary, equations, Disturbing potential, Eccentricity functions, Hansen coefficients ? GRACE?
Published 2010
Journal Vixra
Volume Astrophys Space Sci, Volume 3
No. of pages 7
Abstract
We study the effects of a non-singular gravitational potential on satellite orbits by deriving the corresponding time rates of change of its orbital elements. This is achieved by expanding the non-singular potential into power series up to second order. This series contains three terms, the first been the Newtonian potential and the other two, here R1 (first order term) and R2 (second order term), express deviations of the singular potential from the Newtonian. These deviations from the Newtonian potential are taken as disturbing potential terms in the Lagrange planetary equations that provide the time rates of change of the orbital elements of a satellite in a non-singular gravitational field. We split these effects into secular, low and high frequency components and we evaluate them numerically using the low Earth orbiting mission Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE). We show that the secular effect of the secondorder disturbing term R2 on the perigee and the mean anomaly are 4 .307 ? 10−9/a, and −2 .533 ? 10−15/a, respectively. These effects are far too small and most likely cannot easily be observed with today's technology. Numerical evaluation of the low and high frequency effects of the disturbing term R2 on low Earth orbiters like GRACE are very small and undetectable by current observational means

Saturday Morning Science Chat for those critical thinkers in science not afraid to take on the establishment.
Summary
Nobody came into the live room, so Franklin Hu ran what he called a mailbag: reading out the week's email correspondence on the nature of light and answering it, with comments coming in from the stream. Carl was on air; Roger Anderton was watching. It is a one-sided session, but it collects the arguments Hu returns to more compactly than any other.
Rydin's questions
Roger Rydin had asked the fundamental questions. He had come to think an ether must exist but be uniform everywhere — in which case, how does it pass light? What is disturbed, and what gives back? At best a photon is a wavelet, a short piece of wave, carrying energy and momentum but no mass; individual events like photoelectric absorption, Compton scattering and pair production add up to what we call light waves — but are they really waves? Might light and gravity simply be there , one passing and the other static, without all the supporting machinery? We have invented wave mechanics to help us visualise a process, he wrote, and that does not make it so.

Gravity as a form of light. The parallels are strong — both travel indefinitely, both fall off as one over r ² — and if gravity is a frequency of light, its unlimited range is explained. His image: every pinprick of starlight we can see represents a gravitational source whose field reaches us by exactly the same means.

Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Ian Cohen, James Keene , Stoyan Sarg , Cornelis Verhey , Bob and Jim, with comments from Harry Ricker , Curt Renshaw and Alistair Riddoch on the stream. The topic had been running all week on the email list: the standard textbook picture of an electromagnetic wave — electric and magnetic vectors at right angles, in phase, propagating through empty space — and whether anything of the sort actually happens. Hu put the diagram on screen and asked the room.
The objections to the picture
Bob had two. The first is energy: square the two fields and add them, and the total goes to zero at the nodes and back to a maximum, which he cannot reconcile with conservation. The second came from his reading of Jefimenko , who argues that Maxwell's equations are not causal. Once retardation is put in properly, a changing electric field does not cause a changing magnetic field, nor the reverse; the charges are the source of both, and the two merely propagate together, which is why they look like cause and effect. He added that the picture omits the longitudinal Coulomb component that an oscillating source charge must produce.
Hu pressed the same point geometrically. If there is a source, the field should fall off as the inverse square, which the picture does not show; and the only way to get vectors pointing uniformly perpendicular, rather than radially from a point, would be a flat charged plate cycling between plus and minus five volts, with a rectangular magnet reversing alongside it. He said he found that hard to believe.

Dissidents make a practice of questioning consensus in physics; medicine now presents an international consensus of the same kind, with politicians deferring wholly to it. Is scepticism appropriate here, or irresponsible? His own answer was that the human pressures are identical — careers ended for stepping out of line, funding tied to producing the expected numbers — and that if anything they operate more strongly in a less exact science. He drew a list of what he called secular apocalypses he had lived through: acid rain, the ozone hole, the exhaustion of fossil fuels, Y2K, global warming and then climate change, SARS and Ebola, weapons of mass destruction — each in its turn the end of the world, each questionable only at the sceptic's cost.
Ricker's version was drier: we are at the bottom of the food chain, told to believe the media, which produces experts, who are presumed to know. Whether certified experts can be wrong is the legitimate question, and we cannot tell from here.
Hu's own scepticism was narrower and concrete. He could not reconcile the advice not to wear masks with the effort to secure masks for health workers, nor with other countries handing them out; and the shortages had not eased in weeks. Viscosity, and what it says about mass
Ian's puzzle: liquids grow less viscous as they warm — treacle in January against treacle in June, the oil in an engine — but gases do the opposite, and he had checked it twice, latterly against Jeans's Dynamical Theory of Gases , because it sounded wrong. Nobody in the room could account for the inversion; Hu had expected heat to loosen the bonds in both cases.
Hu's way of thinking about it was mechanical: a rack dragged across a table crowded with billiard balls, the resistance set by how many balls are in the way; add glue to the balls and the sticking matters more when they move slowly, which gives the liquid behaviour. The discussion passed through what distinguishes a solid from a liquid — Hu's criterion being that the bonds hold their geometry regardless of external energy, which is why one solid will not pass through another — and Ian's correction that the state is not a property of the substance, since water takes all three.
That produced the session's key move. If a spoon meets more resistance in molasses than in water, and mass is defined by force over acceleration, then the mass of a marble is not a property of the marble but of the marble against its medium. Hu pressed this deliberately: what he calls matter is the marble; mass is only what we measure when it moves through something.

Summary
David de Hilster hosted a second week in Franklin Hu 's absence, again streaming to both the society's channel and his own Dissident Science , and set the topic deliberately: is charge real?
The case against charge
De Hilster opened with a question few could answer — who first put the plus and minus signs on things? — and gave the answer as Benjamin Franklin. His argument follows from that. The signs are a notation adopted to record which things attract and which repel; they have since become so ingrained that people take charge for an innate property of matter. He regards it instead as a magical attribute imposed on a particle, and asks anyone who uses it for a physical account of what a field actually is. The model he and his father Robert de Hilster are writing up needs no charge at all: the nucleus holds what orbits it for mechanical reasons, everything is Newtonian, and by Occam's razor the burden falls on whoever wants the extra ingredient. He noted that Glenn Borchardt 's neomechanics likewise dispenses with it.
Hu, watching from the road, wrote in twice. First that charge is too complex a phenomenon to be an assumption — which de Hilster read back as an argument for his own side, since an assumption is precisely what one declines to explain. Then that charge needs to emerge as the result of something like ordinary Newtonian physics, at which de Hilster cheerfully declared they agreed.

Keene opened with the video he is planning: clicking through the physics literature at random and noting what it says. His complaint is not that the accounts are wrong so much as that they contradict each other. Elementary particles are defined as those with no smaller constituents — and then CERN papers openly track the breakdown products of the heavy quarks. Grand unification presumes a weak force which he does not regard as a force at all: on his account the weak interactions all rest on the unconditional bit operation, and calling it a force is like calling rust one. The speed of light is listed as a constant of vacuum, whereas his own work has it varying, and requires a minimum quantity of quanta present for light to be conducted at all.
He also gave his reading of magnetic monopoles, which he says need not be a new kind of particle: on his model the L bits are magnetic monopoles, and the reason a divided bar magnet always yields a north and a south is that the division never gets down to the fundamental length constant.

Hu's microphone was barely audible for the first half — a Windows update had reset the level — so Ian carried much of the discussion, and Hu twice handed the chair over while attending to his mother.
Ian: are spiral galaxies spiral?
Ian's proposal, which he has raised before and thinks neglected, is that what we see in the night sky is not a contemporaneous snapshot. An object is visible only if it happened to be at a distance of X light years at the moment X years ago when it emitted the light; if it was elsewhere then, the light has already passed us or has not yet arrived. Looking at a nebula whose near side is a million light years away and whose far side is two million, we are combining events separated by a million years.
From that he draws two conclusions. First, that the gravitational effects attributed to dark matter may simply be matter we cannot see — ordinary matter, of the kind found in a laboratory, that is not at the right distance for its light to reach us now. He prefers to call this dark stuff , declining the mainstream term. Second, and more provocatively, that spiral galaxies may not be spiral. His tentative position is that they are elliptical or spherical bodies whose apparent shape is the composite of parts seen at different epochs as the object rotates.

Lucas had found a YouTube channel by Robert Distinti, an electrical engineer with a couple of hundred videos, and recommended it as a third party critical of everyone's theories rather than of any one of them. Hu played David de Hilster 's review of Distinti's latest.
The point that stuck was Distinti's rule that a theory's ability does not prove its exclusivity: that a model gives good answers does not show no other model would give the same ones. De Hilster's illustration from his own experience was a dean telling him his thesis was ridiculous because Maxwell's equations are irrefutable — which, he said, misses that there may be another way to arrive at the same place. Distinti's remedy for what he calls polytheism — several theories fitting the same data — is to increase the sampling footprint until the candidates can be told apart, his example being two sine waves of different frequency that both pass through every measured point until one measures more finely.
Lucas drew from it the moral he cared about: a theory is never finished. General relativity was put forward to explain gravity, and when the Pioneer trajectories and the spiral arms did not fit, the response was to add dark matter and dark energy rather than to falsify anything.

Summary
Bob Gray presented an update on his classical electrodynamics research, hosted by Franklin Hu , with Bill Lucas , Ian Cohen, James Keene and Alistair Riddoch taking part.
Gray: from Weber to a generalized Maxwell system
Gray is looking for the simplest and most complete route to classical electrodynamics. His starting point is Weber electrodynamics, which is conventionally presented without fields at all: everything follows from a single potential energy function. He has taken that function and defined fields and potentials from it, arriving at four equations that look much like Maxwell's but carry three extra terms. Those terms come from the time derivative of the charge density, which appears in Weber's approach and, for reasons he cannot see, not in Maxwell's; set them to zero and the two systems coincide. He treats this as evidence that Maxwell's system comes up short.
What he wants and cannot yet get is the expression for the electrodynamic field that he was taught comes from special relativity. He would rather not import relativity into Weber to obtain it, and he reported a correction to his own understanding: Heaviside derived that same expression from Maxwell's equations in 1888, seventeen years before the relativity paper, so it does not depend on relativity at all. Lucas's The Universal Force derives it too, from six empirical laws of electrodynamics — more assumptions than Weber's one potential function, which is why Gray keeps looking.

He asked from the floor why no terrestrial experiment had been contemplated, and then put his own position: that general relativity as such — the space-time account — has not been verified, only certain peripheral anomalies. Coles replied that if one neglects all the evidence then of course there is no evidence, and the audience applauded. Ian's own description of the moment was fair to both sides: the speaker had said all the right things about science being open to question, was not hostile, and was courteous afterwards in the pub, but was plainly reluctant to engage, and the applause was for putting down a crank at the back.
He pressed two further points privately. On the standard rejoinder that GPS confirms general relativity daily, he answered that what GPS shows is the variation of atomic clock rates with gravitational potential, which is not general relativity as such; and he said that GPS contradicts special relativity, since the speed of light there is not independent of the observer's motion. Infinity, and immutability
Riddoch opened with two things he had been turning over. The first was density: he had learned that relativity has the centre of a black hole infinitely dense, and wanted to know whether infinite density is even a possible thing. Hu's answer was that an infinity in a result is a red flag that something has gone wrong, and he made the same complaint about renormalization, which he calls dividing one infinity by another and keeping the answer. Ian agreed — thou shalt not divide by zero — and extended it to the big bang's infinitely small interval and infinitely great density, and to the Copenhagen picture, which appears to require an infinite speed of transmission where relativity has a finite one.
The second was the word immutable . Riddoch's own model has Planck-scale building blocks that have always existed and never change: not permeable, not compressible, not flexible. What changes is only their relative orientation, spin polarity and rate of rotation. Because they are not perfect spheres — their surfaces are wave-deformed — the gaps between them do change, alternating between hyperbolic tetrahedra and hyperbolic octahedra as the blocks turn. Those gaps are genuine void, with no properties at all except a shape, and the shape is defined entirely from outside: as he put it, it is the doughnut that defines the hole, not the hole.

Eugene: a biogenic origin for earthquakes
Eugene presented what he calls the biogenic earthquake hypothesis, posted as a preprint on EarthArXiv: that microbial life beneath the surface may trigger earthquakes.
His argument runs in stages. The accepted limit on the depth of the biosphere — twelve to fifteen kilometres — rests on temperature and pressure limits he thinks badly underestimated: the most extreme organism known before 2018 tolerated 122 to 130 °C, and a strain found that year survives well beyond it. Set against models of the earth's interior composition, he arrives at a possible limit near seventy-five kilometres, which is deep enough to matter for earthquakes.
For how such organisms would feed, he pointed to a documented case: bacterial chains beneath the ocean floor that perform a distributed respiration, the deeper cells taking electrons from sulphur and passing them up the chain to cells at the surface that attach them to oxygen — effectively feeding on an electric current. He suggests telluric currents could do the same tens of kilometres down. He also gave energy estimates that he says are adequate even for a magnitude nine event.

Bob Gray presented on the internal consistency of Maxwell's equations, hosted by Franklin Hu , with Bill Lucas , Harry Ricker , James Keene , Cornelis Verhey , Carl and, later, David de Hilster .
Gray's claim
Gray had been working from Frederick David Tombe 's account of Maxwell's original equations, drawn from the 1861 and 1864 papers — twenty equations, presented in vector notation as eight. His question is not whether the equations agree with experiment but whether they are mathematically consistent among themselves: can one show, for a given equation, that the left-hand side genuinely equals the right?
To ask that he had to add assumptions, which he listed and offered for challenge: vacuum permittivity and permeability, one constitutive relation Tombe omits, point charges as an adequate approximation to their positions, the charge density as a sum of delta functions, the current density as charge density times a velocity, and expressions for the scalar and vector potentials for discrete charges. Everything then stands in fundamental quantities and the check can be made.
His result: it fails. Working out the divergence of E with those substitutions yields, on the right, a term containing the accelerations of the charges — the vector potential involves the current density, hence velocity, hence a time derivative giving acceleration — and there is nothing corresponding on the left. So the two sides cannot be equal in general.

The paper reported the first space-based measurement: the MESSENGER spacecraft carries a neutron detector, and neutrons knocked out of Venus and Mercury by cosmic rays and counted at altitude give an estimate of how long they survive.
Hu set out why the item matters. The two laboratory methods — the bottle and the beam — do not agree: the beam gives about nine seconds longer than the bottle, against a lifetime near fourteen and a half minutes. If both are equally valid and give different answers, what is being measured? He returned to this as his standing test case, alongside the gravitational constant. He also noted how remarkable the number itself is: fourteen minutes is an age for a subatomic particle, closer to the decay of an atomic nucleus than to a muon. And he explained why the measurement is hard at all: a free neutron is nearly undetectable, and a detector is essentially a counter tube wrapped in a large block of wax, registering what the neutrons produce rather than the neutrons.
The verdict on the new result was that its uncertainty — something like ten to seventeen minutes — is far too wide to choose between the two laboratory values, though the group hopes to build a more precise instrument.

An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with James Keene , Ian Cohen, Alistair Riddoch , Carl and Bob Gray . It began with the clocks — Ian had arrived an hour early, the American and European changeovers being a fortnight apart — and with his account of daylight saving as a German wartime measure of 1916 to save coal, copied by Britain a month later. From the clocks it went to time itself and stayed there.
Is time quantized?
Keene holds that space, time and energy are all quantized, and that this is what makes his binary mechanics work: with those three quantities discrete, the quantities usually presented to students as fundamental physical constants become derivable rather than merely measured. He put the criterion plainly — by their fruits ye shall know them — and treated the quantization as a postulate justified by its utility, declining to go behind it. Asked why the world should be quantized, he said that is where science shades into philosophy and religion, and that he would leave it to others; he noted that Bill Lucas , asked the same, answers that God made it so, and that this is not where he himself will go.
Hu wanted a physical cause rather than a postulate, and offered one: that we are inside a computer. Nothing in a computer happens faster than the clock; each tick fixes a state; a bit is here or there and never half-way. Keene was sympathetic but said this is only another way of saying that space, time and energy are quantized.

The shape of the photon
Hu repeated the claim he had made the previous week — that a photon occupies the space of a rod, still a compression wave, with the rod's orientation carrying the polarisation — and drew from it the distinction he thinks matters. At the high-frequency end everything looks like particles; at the radio end everything looks like waves; and that, he argued, is not a continuum of behaviour but two different things. Light generated by atomic electron transitions comes in these rod-like packets of fixed energy; a radio wave is more like an ocean wave, broad and of any amplitude.
Harry Ricker pressed the obvious objection: the electromagnetic spectrum appears continuous, from the very low frequencies once used to reach submerged submarines up to the extreme high frequencies — so where does one behaviour stop and the other begin? Hu's answer was that the boundary is technological, set by how fast electrons can be made to oscillate in a circuit, and he asked repeatedly what the highest radio frequency actually achievable is and where it sits on the spectrum. Ricker's own answer was that the spectrum is one thing described by two different models at the two ends, that the choice is a matter of which model one is using, and that this does not answer what either a photon or a radio wave physically is.

What is wrong with QED
Bob's summary of the paper's complaint was mathematical. Any QED calculation runs into infinities, and what is done with them depends on how the sums are taken and what is subtracted from what. The paper's first equation is the assignment of −1/12 to the sum of all the positive integers — traceable, through its references, to Euler — and this is used in the course of a calculation held up as physics' most accurate. Hu made the same complaint about renormalization: dividing infinity by infinity and keeping the answer.
The session then worked through the encyclopaedia articles on quantum electrodynamics, the quantum vacuum and the anomalous magnetic moment, reading them aloud. Hu could make nothing of the Feynman diagram — an electron and positron annihilating to a gamma ray which then produces a quark, an antiquark and a gluon, three things he takes not to exist — and said it looked like a cartoon.
Keene's objection went to the physics rather than the arithmetic. Most of what is going on, he said, is hidden in the diagram's vertices: when he derives Planck's constant from first principles it comes out as an elemental action divided by the fine structure constant, which implies well over a hundred events inside what is treated as a single Planck-constant event.

Summary
A general science chat hosted by Franklin Hu , standing in with no speaker scheduled, and used to make the first public presentation of an idea he had arrived at two or three months earlier. He stated it without preamble: the shape of a photon is a rod.
Why a shape at all
Hu's argument for insisting on one is that he is a physicalist — if it cannot be shown on a billiard table he does not believe it — and that the history of the DNA molecule is the model. The components were known long before anyone found the arrangement that fitted the data, and the helix ended the mystery. He wants the same for light rather than talk of a photon whose shape nobody will state.
A rod that is a wave
His second claim is that light is strictly a wave: he does not accept wave–particle duality, and says so rather than working around it. What he means by a rod is the wavelet one would get by dipping a rectangular object into a very narrow wave tank — a single pulse with a fixed width and height travelling in a straight line, not the great circular waves one normally makes.
He listed the properties this has to account for: light travels in rays, it does not disperse, and it is localised. His example was pair annihilation, where two back-to-back gamma rays strike specific spots in a silicon detector rather than smearing across it. A rod, he argued, has all three particle-like properties and remains a wave.
The inverse square law he handled by distinguishing the individual photon from the population: a photon from Alpha Centauri arrives at full amplitude, and it is only the number per unit area that thins with distance.

The available escape — that the clumps are so small that collisions are effectively never — he thought strained, since the interaction appears to be not nearly zero but exactly zero. On a wave view it follows without effort: the medium's particles have more than one degree of freedom, so a displacement from one direction and a displacement from another can be carried at once. He added the stronger version: two water waves meeting head-on rise together and pass straight through each other, which no two solid objects do — a white brick meeting a red brick stops.

Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with James Keene and Bob Gray , most of it a sustained and good-tempered argument between Hu and Keene about what counts as an explanation.
Deriving the constants
Keene's claim for binary mechanics is that it derives what are called the fundamental constants — the speed of light, Planck's constant, the electron mass and others — from first principles, and that nobody else does. His first principles he described as minimal: the full quantisation of space, time and energy, quantisation being already accepted for charge.
The distinction he insisted on, and which Hu eventually accepted as a clean statement of where they differ, is between deriving a constant and showing interrelationships among constants. The literature is full of formulae relating the fine structure constant, the charge, the speed of light and the rest to one another, and Keene has no quarrel with that work — it is simply, as he put it, a different cage in the zoo. His rule is that unexplained data may not be explained by reference to other unexplained data. He noted, as support rather than opposition, that the standard model concedes it cannot derive any of these constants from its own principles.
Hu's counter, pressed several times, was that binary mechanics grounds out the same way one level down: it takes fundamental quantities of length, time and mass, and cannot say where those come from. Keene agreed without embarrassment — he has not attempted to, and there is an empty slot for anyone who wants to. Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Dennis Allen , Bob, Roger, Bill Lucas , Alistair Riddoch and Ian Cohen, taking up an argument running on the society's email list.
Do a heavy and a light object really fall together?
Ian Cohen set out the case, carefully and at length, that they do not quite. The textbook derivation cancels the small mass from both sides and leaves the acceleration as GM/r ²; but the earth is not stationary, and the object attracts it too, so the relative acceleration is G(M+m)/r ². Two consequences follow. The heavier object accelerates very slightly faster. And, if the two experiments are run one after the other, the heavier object has slightly less distance to cover, because the earth has moved further to meet it. He was emphatic that this is not Aristotle vindicated — the difference is of the order of the object's mass to the earth's — but that it is not exactly zero either.
Hu accepted the distance argument readily and resisted the acceleration one, on the ground that inertial resistance rises in proportion to the force. Ian took him through it again, and the disagreement did not resolve.
Riddoch made the observation that clarified the case: if both objects are released at the same moment, the earth's movement toward them is common to both, so that effect drops out and only the acceleration difference remains — which is exactly the thought experiment Ian had proposed. He then scaled it up memorably: if the whole human population jumped a metre at once, the earth would move about a twelve-trillionth of a metre the other way, and when one person alone jumps, it moves eight billion times less.

Bob brought a paper he thought the group should see: a Liverpool group's experimental test of electron beam deflection in the fringing field of a solenoid, comparing three predictions — Weber's force equation, the Maxwell–Lorentz field treatment, and a commercial boundary-element package.
The result, which he showed from the plotted data, is that in the low velocity regime the Weber prediction tracks the measured deflections closely across three solenoid sizes while the Lorentz prediction is well off. Bob was careful to keep his own enthusiasm in check: he is a Weber partisan and said so, and added that Weber does not fit everything — at velocities near the speed of light it fails and the Lorentz treatment with the relativistic factor does better. His own standing question was why there is not one equation that works everywhere.
Hu found the more striking point to be that a law as basic as the Lorentz force is not confirmed here, and asked whether the paper had done the high-speed experiments itself. Bob was scrupulous: the paper cites others for that and he did not know how those were set up, so he would not speak for the authors.
The two then drew out the methodological difference. The exchange had been running for some weeks and this session was Hu's response to the response.
The disagreement
Gary's position, as Hu set it out from the video, is that light is strictly a particle: photons drawn as circles, with the polarisation an inherent property of each, no waves anywhere, and radio behaving the same way. Hu's is that a photon is a wavelet in a medium.
Hu was at pains to say how much he agrees. Treating photons as discrete clumps travelling through space with a definite volume and length is right; so is the account of what they do on arrival, jostling electrons; so is the photoelectric explanation, that what matters is the energy delivered per unit time rather than the total, with the fixed quantum hv per packet. His own picture of the photon as a rod maps onto Gary's circles, the rod's orientation supplying the polarisation.
His criticism is that the account is incomplete rather than wrong: it has to postulate a photon that stands in no relation to anything else known, and cannot say what it is made of. He used his standing image for this — the socks disappearing from the dryer, which little elves would explain perfectly consistently and without any way of being tested. Logical consistency, he said, is grossly insufficient. His own theory, he argued, sits one level below Gary's and says what the clump is.

Bob's answer: there is no magnetic field
Bob's case, developed over a long presentation, is that the magnetic field is not a physical field at all.
He began with terminology — field means several different things, and if one defines an electrodynamic field as force per unit charge on a test body, then B does not qualify, its units being wrong.
His alternative comes from Weber electrodynamics, where the force between two charged bodies is the Coulomb force multiplied by a coupling coefficient with a constant term, a velocity-dependent term and an acceleration-dependent term. His analogy was static against kinetic friction: nobody finds it strange that the coupling between two objects differs according to their relative motion. On this reading the magnetic field is simply that dynamic coupling, and the Coulomb field is the only real physical field.
He applied Occam's razor twice. First to William J Hooper , who identifies three electric fields — Coulomb, motional and transformer — which Bob tabulated to show that they differ precisely in how many time derivatives they carry: none, one, two. Second to the multipole expansion of the scalar potential, whose infinite series of terms would, on the same logic, give an infinite series of fields.

Is faster-than-light travel possible?
Hu put the question round the room before showing the article.
Ian Cohen had no objection in principle: the speed of light is an arbitrary speed much as the speed of sound in air is, being the speed of electromagnetic radiation in the ether, and there is no reason nothing should exceed it. He drew a distinction that ran through the session — between exceeding c by orders of magnitude, which is the science-fiction case, and exceeding it slightly, which needs only a refractive index below unity. His own example is the total internal reflection of radio waves at the ionosphere, where the phase speed exceeds c by a few per cent. He also holds, as a standing position, that gravitational interaction propagates far faster than light.
Bill Lucas framed it as a question about the medium: c reflects the tensile strength of the electromagnetic field, as measured by Hooper , so the question is whether that strength can differ — and he has seen no answer.

Ian Cohen's account
Asked for his background, Ian gave it at length. He is an engineering scientist from Dublin with degrees in engineering and mathematics, and a doctorate in mathematical modelling and computer simulation of the thermal response of buildings, done during the first energy crisis. He remembers being struck at eighteen, in a first-year physics course, by the reciprocity paradox in special relativity — the question Dingle put, how a clock can be both faster and slower — and finding the answers unsatisfactory; but he went on with the mainstream.
What turned him was Al Kelly . In the early to mid nineties Kelly gave lectures in Dublin, the first at Trinity College, Ian's own university, arguing from the Sagnac effect that the postulates of special relativity are suspect — an effect Ian had never been taught. He went, found colleagues in the audience dismissive, and was struck enough to look into it: the alternative readings of Michelson–Morley, an ether travelling with the earth in its orbit. There followed a correspondence in the Irish Times between Kelly and the academic community, including the Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies — founded in 1940 by de Valera on the model of Princeton's — whose replies Ian described as hostile and insulting.

Summary
John B Eichler — a computer scientist from the Illinois Institute of Technology who worked on Univac machines in the vacuum-tube era and designed blast shields for the Atomic Energy Commission — presenting the connection he sees between cosmology and expansion tectonics: that one must know how the solar system was assembled to understand what is happening to the earth.
Method
He began with what he thinks goes wrong. Where hands-on experiment is possible, results repeat; the earth and the universe do not allow it, and the strongest evidence is where laboratory work backs the theoretical construct. So one should question any proposed esoteric law that has no empirical verification, and remember that a concept being visualisable does not make it obey the laws of physics.
He then defined worldview as what the scientist brings to the table — the paradigms absorbed from classes and books. These are two-edged: without a framework we could not make sense of anything, and with one we cannot see past it. To a hammer, everything looks like a nail.

Abstract
A new cosmological theory is presented based on the proposition that all four metrical coefficients of space and time change with the cosmological expansion. Such a universal scale expansion would preserve the four-dimensional spacetime geometry and therefore by general relativity most physical relationships. In addition, if the scale expansion were exponential with time, all epochs would be equivalent. The theory resolves several outstanding problems with the Big Bang theory and better agrees with four observational programs. It also provides a simple explanation to the Pioneer anomaly.
Overview
This is the first of a projected four-part series in Apeiron in which C Johan Masreliez sets out the Scale Expanding Cosmos (SEC) theory. Its founding proposition is a single change to the standard cosmological line element: instead of expanding only the three spatial metrical coefficients, as Friedmann's choice of coordinates does, let all four — space and time together — expand by a common exponential factor. Abstract
In a previous article the author introduced the Scale Expanding Cosmos (SEC) theory and showed that this new theory could resolve several problems with the Standard Cosmological Model. This new theory better agrees with observational data, for example the number count test, the angular size test, the surface brightness test and the supernovae Ia observations. In addition it provides a simple explanation to the Pioneer anomaly. The SEC theory predicts new and testable cosmological features among them cosmic (velocity) drag, which is the subject of this paper. I will show that currently there is substantial evidence for cosmic drag and suggest how this new and unexpected aspect of the universe may be confirmed by observations in the solar system.

Summary
James Keene on quantum entanglement and Bell's theorem, hosted by Franklin Hu , with Bob Gray , Ian Cohen, Roger, Carl and Bill Lucas present.
The argument
Keene's paper takes its stand on a remark of Bell's own: that there is a way to escape the inference of superluminal speeds and spooky action at a distance, but that it involves absolute determinism. That escape is the freedom loophole , and Keene's claim is that binary mechanics occupies it — a local realist theory with exact time development laws, in which all action occurs over one length constant in one time constant, and in which the one-state quanta exist whether observed or not.
The consequence he draws is that entanglement experiments cannot settle the matter by themselves. Closing every other loophole leaves this one; to close it one would have to falsify the local realist theory directly — that is, falsify the quantisation of space, time and energy.
He was scathing about how the loophole is discussed, and this was the liveliest part of the paper: not merely deterministic but super -deterministic; not merely determinism but absolute determinism; not merely hard to imagine but impossible; not merely a question about free will but a loss of freedom to choose ; not merely a new question but unscientific. He called the vocabulary a propaganda ploy — believe in superluminal effects or be an anti-freedom jerk — and said the reason for it is precisely that the experiments alone cannot exclude the alternative.

Dmitriev's weight measurements
The experiments are Alexander Dmitriev's, at the technical university in St Petersburg, and Keene presented them as work that stands or falls on its own merits whatever anyone thinks of his interpretation.
They are all high-precision weighings of sealed containers in which something is stimulated. A brass rod heated ultrasonically loses weight over the period of heating. A piezoceramic pile heated by one degree shows the container's apparent mass fall while the temperature is held up, and stay down as long as it is held. Coils of optical fibre illuminated by helium and semiconductor lasers lose weight while the light is passing, and recover it a few seconds after the laser is switched off. And a container holding two rotors spinning in opposite directions — so that the total angular momentum is about zero — shows a mass difference that grows with the frequency of rotation.
On the last, Keene had written to Dmitriev because he could not tell from the paper which orientation weighed less, having predicted in the same email that it would be the horizontal rotor; the reply arrived a quarter of an hour before the session and confirmed it. Hu pressed him repeatedly and with some exasperation on what horizontal means — the plane of the spinning disc or the axis — and the answer settled on the axis lying parallel to the earth's surface.

Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Bill Lucas , Ian Cohen, James Keene , Alistair Riddoch and Dennis Allen . Hu opened with a question rather than a topic: it is February 2020, a date that once sounded futuristic — why are there still such holes in physics, and why does nobody, orthodox or otherwise, know what gravity is?
Lucas on why
Lucas's answer was historical and political. He traced it to the American settlement between the established colonial churches and the revival movements, and argued that from about 1850 the separation of church and state was used to license a science defined by opposition to religion: what Maxwell and Ampère had called the Spirit of God became the electric field, and quantum mechanics took the universal wave function rather than the field as its object. He credited Poincaré with a meta-theory of theorems from logic applicable to all scientific theories, said Poincaré published relativity a year before Einstein and then showed by those theorems that it was false, and that this was why the theory was carried elsewhere.
He gave his own experience as evidence of the cost. He had held the highest-paid postdoctoral position in the country at Catholic University, running a National Science Foundation grant to treat a thousand inoperable brain tumours with negative pion beams made at Los Alamos — the pion stopping in the brain, replacing an electron, entering the nucleus and breaking it up — with 990 of the thousand tumours destroyed and no notable side effects; and he was dismissed by the NSF and the Department of Energy after giving a paper to the American Physical Society arguing that logic falsifies special and general relativity. Scott A. Mainwaring is an American consultant and philanthropist based in Helena, Montana, who is known within Electric Universe circles as a principal supporter and co-founder of the SAFIRE Project, an experimental effort to test the Electric Sun model.
Biography
Mainwaring resides in Helena, Montana, where he has worked as a consultant and part-time lecturer. He is the son of Bruce Mainwaring, a longtime advocate of the Electric Universe idea, and together they have directed the Mainwaring Archive Foundation, the philanthropic vehicle through which the family has funded independent scientific research.
Mainwaring became involved in Electric Universe research after attending the 2012 Electric Universe conference, where he encountered the proposal of engineer Montgomery Childs to build an apparatus capable of testing the Electric Sun hypothesis empirically.
Work
Mainwaring recognized in Montgomery Childs' proposal a pragmatic, empirical method for testing the Electric Universe hypothesis, and in particular the Electric Sun model. He introduced the proposal to his father, Bruce Mainwaring, and the two decided to support the initiative through the Mainwaring Archive Foundation.
The resulting effort became the SAFIRE Project, which sought to reproduce and study, in the laboratory, plasma conditions resembling those proposed for the Sun. The project proceeded through a bench-top proof-of-concept phase, a full-scale laboratory phase built around the "SAFIRE Plasma Engine," and subsequent research into the molecular and atomic-scale reactions observed in its plasma environments. Beyond financing the work, Mainwaring consulted regularly with Childs and contributed hands-on assistance during construction of the Phase 2 apparatus.
The SAFIRE Project was later carried forward as a commercial enterprise under Aureon Energy Ltd.

Abstract
Gravitational waves, like EM waves , can be used to transport intelligent signals. Alien civilizations may be advanced enough to have discovered how to generate (and/or modulate ) gravitational waves. These waves could be detected using gravitational wave detector technology. Gravitational waves would probably be the preferred method of extraterrestrial communication for the following reasons:
They can be monitored 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, regardless of weather conditions.
Gravitational waves are more like sound waves, which can be detected (or heard), regardless of detector orientation.

Roger J Anderton hosted this himself, continuing from his sessions on Minkowski spacetime. He cited Alexander Unzicker as holding that the development went wrong in exactly that decade.
