title: Sloan Digital Sky Survey
content_preview:
The Sloan Digital Sky Survey ( SDSS ) is a long-running imaging and spectroscopic survey of the sky, begun in 2000 and named for the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, which funded it. It is the source of much of the observational material that arguments about redshift , quasars and large-scale structure have been conducted on for the past twenty-five years — including a number of the arguments recorded on this wiki.
This article is a short account of the survey oriented to that use. It describes what SDSS is and where it now stands, and then sets out the particular data products that pages on this wiki draw on, and what the disputes over them have been.
The survey
SDSS observes with two telescopes: the Sloan Foundation 2.5 m telescope at Apache Point Observatory in New Mexico, which has carried the survey since the beginning, and the du Pont 2.5 m telescope at Las Campanas Observatory in Chile, which extends it to the southern sky.
Its work divides into two kinds. Imaging records the positions, brightnesses and colours of objects; the imaging camera was retired in 2009, by which time the survey had photometered several hundred million objects over roughly a third of the sky. Spectroscopy — now the whole of the survey's activity — measures the spectrum of a selected object, which is what yields a redshift and hence, on the standard interpretation, a distance.
The survey has run in five phases:
SDSS-I (2000–2005) — the original imaging and redshift survey
SDSS-II (2005–2008) — adding a Milky Way structure survey and the Sloan Supernova Survey
SDSS-III (2008–2014) — including BOSS, the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey
SDSS-IV (2014–2020) — extending to the southern hemisphere
SDSS-V (2020– ) — the current phase, organised as three "mappers": the Milky Way Mapper , the Black Hole Mapper (a time-domain spectroscopic survey of quasars and X-ray sources) and the Local Volume Mapper

The Society for the Advancement of Autodynamics (SAA) was founded in 1994 in Southern California by David de Hilster , Dr. Ricardo Carezani , Amnon Meyers and others, with the purpose of advancing the theory of Autodynamics as developed by Carezani. It later had a chapter in the United Kingdom, and it remains the publisher of essentially the whole Autodynamics literature.
Activities
Publishing
The Society produced a book early on but sold only a few copies. Its two substantial titles are Autodynamics: Fundamental Basis for a New Relativistic Mechanics (1998), the first comprehensive statement of the theory, and Autodynamics: Storm in Physics (2005). The 1998 book was the first to be mass-printed, putting copies into the thousands.
Beyond the books, the Society publishes Carezani's papers, derivations and expository notes at autodynamics.org . That collection is indexed at Ricardo L Carezani and grouped by subject at Autodynamics ; it includes the derivations ( Frames Derivation , Galilean Simplification , The Superfluous System ), the decay papers ( Muon Decay and Autodynamics , Pion Decay and Autodynamics , Nucleus-Nucleus Collision , The Compton Effect and Autodynamics ), the gravitational programme ( Universal Gravitation in Autodynamics and its four applications), and the neutrino papers ( Origin of the Neutrino , Super-Kamiokande: Super-Proof for Neutrino Non-existence , Neutrinos at Fermi Lab , SN 1987A and the Neutrino ).
Several members appear as authors or editors across that body of work: Lucy Haye as co-author of the astrophysical papers, de Hilster and Meyers as editors, and Brian F. Hall as editor of the Pioneer paper.

The Society has twice intervened publicly against the neutrino hypothesis. Abstract
Still more shocking than the metaphysical assumption of some initial singularity, is the constant insistence upon the so-called cosmological principle of "homogeneity" and "isotropy" of the Universe. Observations do contradict this principle. And to me, the inhomogeneous, fractal at least on a certain scale range, of the distribution of matter is in itself an important cosmological fact, hitherto almost neglected. Moreover difficultties as to the applicability of the second principle of thermodynamics, observations of abnormal redshifts, etc., are casting large doubts not only upon the standard cosmological models, but even on the interpretation of the observed redshift as due solely to a universal expansion.
Overview
Pecker's paper is a conference contribution — delivered to a meeting at which Halton Arp , Jayant Narlikar and Geoffrey Burbidge also spoke — setting out, from the standpoint of a senior professional astronomer at the Collège de France, why he had never accepted the Big Bang . It is not a paper proposing an alternative model. It is a catalogue of the assumptions he regards as unearned, arranged as five complaints: the initial singularity, the cosmological principle, the arbitrary selection of "significant" facts, the unexamined application of the second law of thermodynamics to the universe as a whole, and the accumulating evidence of anomalous Redshifts .
His central objection is methodological. The standard model, he argues, rests less on observation than on a demand for simplicity — "the argument of simplicity is a Pythagorician argument, which cannot convince" — and Occam's razor is being used not to prune hypotheses but to forbid them. Spacetime curvature is the proposal, central to general relativity , that gravitation is not a force acting between bodies but a property of the geometry through which they move. Mass and energy deform a four-dimensional continuum of space and time; bodies then follow the straightest available paths through that deformed geometry, and what Newton described as an attractive force appears as an artefact of the shape of the arena.
It is the single most disputed idea documented on this wiki. Roughly 184 pages engage with it directly — some 84 papers, 44 scientist biographies and 14 books — and around 450 discuss curvature in some form. That places it above push gravity , tired light and the Casimir effect in the volume of material collected here.
What the standard account claims
Albert Einstein 's field equations relate the curvature of spacetime at a point to the energy and momentum present there. The account is economical: one geometric statement replaces both the gravitational force and the flat background of special relativity, and it has passed every precision test put to it, from the perihelion advance of Mercury and the bending of starlight to the Shapiro delay, gravitational redshift, frame dragging, the orbital decay of binary pulsars and the direct detection of gravitational waves in 2015.
Its critics do not generally dispute those measurements. What they dispute is the interpretation — whether geometry is the cause of gravitation or merely an efficient bookkeeping for it.

The paper turns on a distinction that governs the whole of Autodynamics. Autodynamics, Carezani writes, "was derived to describe decay cases: no external energy or kinetic energy is introduced into the system. All energy comes from the particle itself" — the rocket, whose thrust is bought with its own mass. Special relativity, by contrast, describes energy "applied externally to a particle", so that the total is the rest mass plus a kinetic contribution from outside — the cannon and the cannon ball.
The transformation makes that difference into a substitution.

Substituting, distributing, cancelling the common energy terms and isolating E c returns
E c = m 0 c 2 [ 1 1 − β 2 − 1 ]

Special relativity is the physical theory published by Albert Einstein in 1905 in the paper On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies . It describes the relationship between space and time for observers moving uniformly relative to one another, and it replaced the Galilean transformations of classical mechanics with the Lorentz transformations . In mainstream physics it is regarded as extensively confirmed by experiment.
Special relativity is also the single most-discussed subject on this wiki. It is the keyword of more papers catalogued here than any other concept in physics, and the literature indexed under it — several hundred papers, together with dozens of books — is overwhelmingly critical. The critics are not a single school. They disagree with each other about what is wrong, about what should replace the theory, and about whether anything need replace it at all. What they share is the conviction that the theory's two postulates, its derivation, its treatment of time and simultaneity, or its claimed experimental support will not survive careful examination. This article states the theory briefly and then presents that body of work, author by author and argument by argument.

title: Natural Philosophy Wiki

The speed of light in vacuum, written c , is the most heavily loaded constant in modern physics. It fixes the ratio between mass and energy, sets the scale of the electromagnetic field equations, defines the metre, and — in the form of Einstein's second postulate, that c has the same value in every inertial frame regardless of the motion of the source — supplies the foundation on which special relativity is built. Since the 1983 redefinition of the SI metre, c is no longer measured at all: it is defined as exactly 299,792,458 metres per second, and the metre is derived from it.
The literature collected on this wiki treats almost every part of that account as open. The researchers documented here do not agree with one another — some hold that c is constant but relative to a medium or a field rather than to every observer; some that the two-way speed is constant while the one-way speed is not; some that c varies with gravitational potential, with the medium, or with time; some that the constancy observed in experiments is an artefact of the instruments used to measure it; and a few that the light-speed barrier can be exceeded outright. What they share is the conviction that the second postulate was elevated to a principle before the experimental evidence could bear it, and that the 1983 redefinition has since made the question difficult even to ask, because a discrepant measurement now registers as a wrongly calibrated metre rather than as a physical result.
This article states the orthodox position, then organises the objections found in the archive by the idea at stake rather than by author.
The mainstream position
Three claims are usually run together under the heading "constancy of the speed of light", and the papers here often turn on separating them.

Title Speed of Light in 3-Dimensional Euclidean Space
Read in full Link to paper
Author(s) Nina B Sotina , Nadia Lvov
Keywords relativity , aether
Published 2013
No. of pages 7
Abstract
The speed of light according to the Special Theory of Relativity has the same value C with respect to any inertial frame of reference in 4-dimensional pseudo-Euclidean space. An attempt to build an alternative physical model in 3-dimensional Euclidean space brings up a question: in what frame of reference does light move with the speed C? Series of experiments and mathematical reasoning suggest that: 1) the speed of a photon emitted by an atom equals to C if measured with respect to the atom if the atom is at rest or moving with a constant speed with respect to a 3-dimensional inertial frame of reference; 2) the speed of light acquires the value of a constant C near Earth, Sun and other large masses; the energy of the photon depends on the gravitational potential, 3) light has inertial properties.
Overview
Presented at the 20th Natural Philosophy Alliance conference in 2013, this paper by Nina Sotina and Nadia Lvov asks a question that special relativity dissolves rather than answers: if space is ordinary three-dimensional Euclidean space and time is independent of it, then with respect to what does light travel at c ?
Their answer is a modified emission theory. Light leaves an atom at speed c relative to that atom — Walther Ritz's ballistic hypothesis of 1908 — but does not keep that speed. As it propagates it undergoes what the authors call hidden dynamics : its velocity relaxes toward c in the frame of any large nearby mass, and does so without any loss of energy, the change in speed being compensated by a change in the photon's mass. The relativistic kinematics of Minkowski space is then, on this view, a formalism that gets the right answers by encoding a real dynamical process it does not name.

Stanislav V. Adamenko is a Ukrainian physicist and the founder and scientific director of the Electrodynamics Laboratory "Proton-21" in Kiev, established in 1999.
Work
The laboratory's programme is the pursuit of extreme compression of matter in a small-scale terrestrial apparatus, with the aim of reaching densities approaching those of nuclear matter — conditions Adamenko describes as "stellar" and compares to the interiors of white dwarfs and neutron stars.
The method is a pulsed electron beam of up to a kilojoule, at a few hundred keV and lasting tens of nanoseconds, directed at a solid target a few tens of micrometres across. Adamenko's claim is that this acts as a "coherent driver", initiating a self-organising and self-sustaining collapse of the electron–nucleus plasma, and that the collapse produces a wholesale nuclear rearrangement of part of the target: the synthesis of elements across the whole periodic table, the creation of superheavy nuclei beyond any known element, and the conversion of radioactive nuclei into stable ones. The last of these is presented as a possible route to the treatment of nuclear waste.
The work is set out at length in Controlled Nucleosynthesis: Breakthroughs in Experiment and Theory (Springer, 2007), edited with Vladimir Vysotskii and Andrei Vysotskyy, which collects the laboratory's experimental reports and its theoretical account of the collapse. The programme has been presented mainly at the International Conference on Cold Fusion and Condensed Matter Nuclear Science meetings.
The central experimental claims — in particular the detection of stable nuclei with mass numbers between 250 and 500, and the assertion that a milligram of target material undergoes complete nuclear regeneration in each shot — have not been reproduced elsewhere.

Abstract
As a Bose condensate, superconductors provide novel conditions for revisiting previously proposed couplings between electromagnetism and gravity. Strong variations in Cooper pair density, large conductivity and low magnetic permeability define superconductive and degenerate condensates without the traditional density limits imposed by the Fermi energy (??10−6 g cm 3 ). Recent experiments have reported anomalous weight loss for a test mass suspended above a rotating type II, YBCO superconductor, with the percentage change (0.05-2.1%) independent of the test mass' chemical composition and diamagnetic properties. A variation of 5 parts per 104 was reported above a stationary (non-rotating) superconductor. In experiments using a sensitive gravimeter, bulk YBCO superconductors were stably levitated in a DC magnetic field. Changes in acceleration were measured to be less than 2 parts in 108 of the normal gravitational acceleration. This result puts new limits on the strength and range of the proposed coupling between static superconductors and gravity.

Type Cosmological model
Author(s) Hermann Bondi, Thomas Gold and Fred Hoyle (1948)
Keywords perfect cosmological principle, continuous creation, Big Bang , quasi-steady state , eternal universe
Year 1948
Steady state theory is the cosmological model in which the universe has no beginning and no end, presenting on the large scale the same appearance at every epoch, with new matter created continuously to keep the mean density constant as the universe expands.
The standard account
The theory was put forward in 1948 in two papers in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society : one by Hermann Bondi and Thomas Gold , the other, on a different formal basis, by Fred Hoyle . Its governing assumption is the perfect cosmological principle — the universe is homogeneous and isotropic not only in space, as ordinary cosmology assumes, but also in time. There is therefore no privileged epoch, no "early universe," and no origin event.
The model accepted the observed expansion. To keep the perfect cosmological principle in the face of expansion, matter must appear continuously; the required rate is very small, of the order of one hydrogen atom per cubic metre every billion years, far below any rate that could be detected directly. The universe is thus infinitely old, infinitely extended, and always the same in the mean, with galaxies of every age present everywhere at every time.
The steady state model was the principal rival to the evolving hot-origin cosmology through the 1950s and early 1960s. It was Hoyle who gave the rival theory its name, using the phrase "big bang" dismissively in a 1949 BBC broadcast. The model was falsifiable in a way its rival was not: because it forbids evolution, any evidence that the distant — and therefore earlier — universe differs systematically from the nearby one counts directly against it. The phenomenon of stellar collapse is considered from the viewpoint of the neo-Newtonian ballistic theory of light. The restrictions of the special theory of relativity are thus removed. The theory predicts that a collapsing star will expand again, and continue to alternately expand and collapse at a rate depending on the mass and greatest radius of the star. On each cycle material will be lost, including photons which appear to distant observers as the emissions of a pulsar. It is concluded that pulsars are oscillating stars, that these eventually "evaporate" away completely, and that there is no such object as a black hole.

Waldron's paper, published in Apeiron No. 7 (1990), continues an argument he began in "Do Black Holes Exist?" ( Speculations in Science and Technology , 1983). His original objection was that the gravitational energy released by a collapsing burnt-out star would blow the star apart before it reached the Schwarzschild radius. Correspondence with "a number of leading cosmologists" prompted a rethink, and this paper is the result: instead of an explosion, he now argues for an oscillation . The star collapses, turbulence and rotation halt the infall, it re-expands to nearly its original radius, and the cycle repeats, shedding matter and radiation each time. What a distant observer sees is a pulsar. There is no black hole .
The framework is what Waldron calls the "neo-Newtonian ballistic theory of light" — an emission theory in which Newton's three laws are "inviolable", Einstein's invariance postulate is rejected as "incompatible with the principle of relativity", and light consists of material particles. Steven B. Bryant is an American researcher and technology executive known for a mathematical critique of the derivations underlying special relativity, and for the alternative framework he calls Modern Mechanics (or Modern Classical Mechanics).
His central technical claim concerns Einstein's Spherical Wave Proof . Bryant argues that the proof establishes only that the transformed coordinates satisfy the general equation of a sphere, not that they lie on the same sphere — and that when the radii are checked, the transformed points turn out to lie on multiple spheres rather than one. Since the purpose of the proof is to establish the relationship between the constancy of the speed of light and the principle of relativity, he concludes that the relationship is not established.
His positive proposal turns on a distinction he says relativity conflates: length versus wavelength . On his account time dilation, length contraction and the twin paradox are all artefacts of using a length-based model to interpret wavelength-based observations, and he reports that equations built on the distinction fit the Michelson-Morley and Ives-Stilwell results substantially more closely than the Einstein-Lorentz equations do.
Bryant was a subject matter leader in the relativity community of the Natural Philosophy Alliance , has spoken at AAAS (American Association for the Advancement of Science) and NPA conferences at universities across the United States, and set out his framework for a general readership in Disruptive: Rewriting the Rules of Physics (2016). Steven Dinowitz is an American independent theorist, the author of Field Distortion Theory — an attempt to keep the Galilean transformations while still accounting for the experimental evidence usually taken to establish special relativity .
He is worth attention for a reason that has nothing to do with whether the theory is right. In 1991 he derived from it a specific, numerical, dated prediction about a named experiment — that CERN's Large Electron–Positron collider would prove unable to accelerate an electron past 60 GeV. The machine was built, it ran for nine years, and the prediction can be checked.
Field Distortion Theory
The theory begins with light propagation. Dinowitz proposes that the electric field surrounding a source undergoes an "aerodynamic-like distortion" when the source moves through a gravitational field . The distortion, not a change in the structure of space and time, is what produces the observed behaviour of light; the Galilean transformations are retained throughout, and the theory is offered as consistent with the existing optical evidence while suggesting new experiments.
From there he makes the move the rest depends on: a body's inertial mass is a consequence of that same field distortion . Mass therefore does not increase with velocity as such, but with velocity relative to whichever gravitational field is locally dominant in energy density — near the Earth's surface, the Earth's own field.
The full statement is " Field Distortion Theory (FDT) ", a 26-page paper in Physics Essays 9 (3) in 1996.

Straight Line Motion is a four-page paper by David Tombe , dated 31 May 2018 and posted to the General Science Journal . It inverts the usual order of explanation: rather than treating centrifugal force as a consequence of the tendency to move in a straight line, it treats the straight line as a consequence of centrifugal pressure in a medium.
The medium is Maxwell's, by way of Bernoulli, Tesla and Oliver Lodge, all quoted at length: "space is rendered into tiny whirlpools that are pressing against each other with centrifugal force while striving to dilate." Tombe proposes that in the absence of a radial field "the individual rotation axes of these tiny whirlpools form concentric rings around a moving object", so that the object's line of motion is at right angles to the pressure exerted on it. "When this centrifugal pressure field (inertial field) is symmetrical, the motion will constitute the straight line inertial path."
A key assertion follows: "It's a geometrical fact that a moving object has a centrifugal acceleration to every point in space that does not lie along its path of motion. A supernova is the catastrophic brightening of a star, in which a single object can for a few weeks outshine the whole galaxy that contains it. Supernovae matter far beyond stellar astrophysics because one class of them, Type Ia , is the standard candle on which the modern distance scale — and with it the claim that cosmic expansion is accelerating — rests.
The standard account
Supernovae are sorted spectroscopically. Core-collapse events (Types II, Ib and Ic) are held to occur when a massive star exhausts its nuclear fuel, its iron core collapses, and the infalling envelope rebounds; most of the released energy escapes as neutrinos. Type Ia events show no hydrogen and are attributed instead to the thermonuclear detonation of a white dwarf that has been driven toward the Chandrasekhar mass of about 1.4 solar masses by accretion from, or merger with, a companion.
The nearest supernova of the modern era, SN 1987A in the Large Magellanic Cloud, was seen on 23 February 1987 and remains the only one for which a neutrino burst was detected. Its expanding, strikingly symmetric triple-ring structure has been imaged for decades.
Type Ia events are treated as standardisable candles: their peak brightness correlates with the decline rate of the light curve, so the shape of the curve is used to correct the peak and yield a distance. In 1998 two teams reported that distant Type Ia supernovae appeared fainter than a freely coasting universe predicts, and this was interpreted as accelerating expansion driven by dark energy . A second argument drawn from the same data is that supernova light curves at redshift z appear stretched by a factor of 1+ z , which is presented as a direct observation of cosmological time dilation .

Abstract
The second of two papers arguing that the theory of moving charge carriers cannot explain the electrical conduction of the Hall effect . Part II attacks the concept of the positively charged "hole" as a category mistake, and proposes instead that the sign of the Hall coefficient is governed by crystal structure , within a model in which conduction is the propagation of a state of charge distribution rather than a flow of charges.
The argument against holes
Marinsek's target is the standard account in which conduction in a solid is carried by electrons and by holes — vacancies in a filled band treated as particles of effective positive charge. His objection is not quantitative but conceptual, and he states it as a category mistake : "a successive occurrence of different holes is not identical with the movement of one hole." A hole, on his account, is simply the previous location of an electron; a location cannot move unless the atom moves, which the theory does not claim.
He works this through the "row of seats" analogy used in textbook expositions and in the Wikipedia article on the electron hole, in which people shift one seat along and the empty seat appears to travel the other way. title: The 1855 Weber-Kohlrausch Experiment (The Speed of Light)
content_preview:
Title The 1855 Weber-Kohlrausch Experiment (The Speed of Light)
Read in full Link to paper
Author(s) David Tombe
Published 2019
Journal General Science Journal
Abstract
In the year 1855, German physicists Wilhelm Eduard Weber and Rudolf Kohlrausch performed an experiment with a Leyden jar and established the ratio between electrostatic and electrodynamic units of charge. This ratio became known as Weber’s constant and it is numerically equal to c√2, where c is the speed of light. In 1857, another German physicist Gustav Robert Kirchhoff used Weber’s constant to conclude that electric signals travel along a wire at the speed of light. A few years later in 1861, Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell was working on the physical medium responsible for magnetic lines of force and he had established a linkage between its transverse elasticity and the ratio of electrostatic to electromagnetic units of charge. Electromagnetic units of charge are related to electrodynamic units by a factor of √2. In order to evaluate this ratio, Maxwell looked up Weber’s results, and on converting Weber’s constant into electromagnetic units, the speed of light was exposed. This paper sets out to establish the fundamental origins of the speed of light.
Overview
Dated 14 April 2019 and posted to the General Science Journal , this paper by David Tombe of Northern Ireland is a historical reconstruction with a thesis attached. Its subject is the experiment Wilhelm Weber and Rudolf Kohlrausch performed in 1855, which measured the ratio between the electrostatic and electrodynamic units of charge and so, unexpectedly, produced a velocity.
Tombe traces what followed: Kirchhoff's use of that ratio in 1857 to conclude that electric signals travel along a wire at the speed of light; and Maxwell's use of it in 1861, while working on the elastic medium responsible for magnetic lines of force, to expose the speed of light directly and connect it to the transverse elasticity of the luminiferous medium.

The Reines–Cowan experiment
The statement quotes the Nobel announcement — "There were struggles with the low counting speed and high background. He adds that Bohr's work is "most suggestive, and as marking an epoch in the progress of atomic theory." The dispute is with the theory, not with its author.

The CMB will be discussed from its discovery, and interpretation, to modern satellite measurements including COBE, WMAP, and Plank.
Summary
Having given a session on Lambda-CDM cosmology, Harry Ricker found he could not answer a simple question — what exactly is the cosmic microwave background? — and set out to trace it from the theory to the satellites. His conclusion is about the story rather than the physics: the standard account is constructed by hindsight, and the details do not fit it. Who actually predicted it
The textbooks say Gamow predicted the background and that Penzias and Wilson confirmed it by accident. Ricker went to the sources and found otherwise. Gamow's 1946 paper contains nothing about microwave background radiation; it postulates neutrons decaying into protons and electrons in a hot early state. Alpher and Herman's 1948 paper, which corrects Gamow, gives about 5 K — but for the remnant gas , not for any radiation.
The prediction Ricker credits comes from the Princeton group. Dicke's own account has the hot cosmology in disfavour — probably, Ricker thought, because it could not synthesise the heavier elements — and revived by Hoyle and Tayler's work on helium around 1962. What the Princeton group added, and what is now forgotten, is that their motivation was an oscillating universe: a closed universe contracting to a hot bounce and re-expanding, which avoids having to assume the energy of the universe at t = 0. Abstract
Prior to 1919, general relativity was an obscure theory by a rising star in physics, Albert Einstein. Based on the perceived need to test this complex and intriguing concept, it was held as gospel that the sunlight passing by the sun should be bent by the gravitational attraction of the sun, something known to Sir Isaac Newton and modified by Einstein. According to prevailing wisdom, this should be observable during a total solar eclipse when the shielding of the sun's light permitted the observation of light from distant stars being "bent" around the sun. The Expanding Earth: Some Consequences of Dirac's Gravitation Hypothesis is a 1971 book by the physicist Pascual Jordan , published by Pergamon Press. It is an English translation (by Arthur Beer) of his 1966 German work Die Expansion der Erde (Braunschweig: Friedrich Vieweg).
Overview
Jordan takes up Paul Dirac's "large numbers" hypothesis of a gradual weakening of the gravitational constant G over cosmic time, and works out its geophysical consequences. He argues that, as gravity has weakened, the Earth has slowly expanded — swelling from an initial ball perhaps only about 7,000 km in diameter to its present size — and he connects this to continental drift, the growth of the ocean basins, and other geological evidence. The book is a rare instance of a major theoretical physicist developing the Expanding-Earth idea from a specific cosmological hypothesis.
About the author
Pascual Jordan (1902–1980) was a German theoretical physicist and one of the founders of quantum mechanics and quantum field theory (the Born–Heisenberg–Jordan "three-man paper," and Jordan–Wigner quantization). In his later career he worked on cosmology and gravitation, including scalar-tensor ("Jordan–Brans–Dicke") theories of varying gravity, of which the Expanding Earth was a proposed consequence.

The Farce of Physics is a book by Bryan G Wallace (1933–1997), copyright 1993, arguing that "modern theoretical physics has become to a large degree, little more than an elaborate farce." It is part memoir, part polemic and part sociology of science: an account of Wallace's roughly fifty-year career as a physicist working outside the academic mainstream, organised around his contention that Einstein's second postulate — the constancy of the velocity of light — is contradicted by interplanetary radar data and is the load-bearing assumption of everything built on it.

The central argument
Wallace states the thesis of the book most compactly in Chapter 4, prompted by a reader's question in Marilyn vos Savant's newspaper column about what single discovery would overturn modern science:
Einstein's special relativity theory with his second postulate that the speed of light in space is constant is the linchpin that holds the whole range of modern physics theories together. Shatter this postulate, and modern physics becomes an elaborate farce!
His evidence for shattering it is the one he had pressed since 1969: that published interplanetary radar data, in particular the 1961 radar contact with Venus, fit a classical c + v relative velocity better than a constant c . The book's wider claim is that the physics community's failure to engage with this is not an accident but a symptom — of funding structures, of peer review, and of what he regards as physics having taken on the character of a faith.

This should apply on macroscopic as well as microscopic scales. Implications are extensive particularly in regard to the formation and orbiting of planets, stars, galaxies, and larger formations. Title The Holor Representation of Polarization

"The Holor Representation of Polarization" is a 1994 paper by Domina Eberle Spencer , Uma Y Shama and Terri L Mascardo , published in the Journal of the Illuminating Engineering Society . It applies the algebra of holors to the description of the polarization of light.
Overview
A holor is a mathematical object made up of one or more independent components (called merates ), introduced by Parry Moon and Domina Eberle Spencer in their book Theory of Holors (Cambridge University Press, 1986). The holor concept was proposed as a generalization broad enough to embrace scalars, vectors, matrices, tensors and other multi-component quantities within a single formalism, with a common index notation and a general account of how the components transform. The motivation is that many quantities useful in physics are not tensors, even though the tensor calculus is often treated as the only rigorous framework; holor algebra is offered as a way of handling that wider class of entities on the same footing.
In this paper the authors turn that framework on polarization — the orientation of the transverse oscillations of a light wave. Polarized light is conventionally described in several separate ways: by the two-component complex Jones vector, by the four real Stokes parameters, and by the Mueller matrices that transform them as light passes through optical elements. The paper recasts these descriptions within the holor formalism, giving a unified holor representation of the polarization state and of the operations that act on it. It belongs to a series of works in which Spencer and Moon extended holor methods into physical optics and photometry, the field in which much of their joint work appeared.

Abstract
We introduce the concept of an interface between matter and the dimension of time. This interface will have the form of a surface. We first make the comparison with the way an architect draws a house and its implementation by a builder. The architect may not bother with the thickness of his lines when making the drawing. But the builder must also consider the fine resolution of the lines, which will be enlarged to centimeters or decimeters in practice. Abstract

Here, we analyse if these peaks could be an indication of circling light about the centre of the universe. We find that the Zwicky-Ashmore redshift theory provides an excellent evidence for circling light. We can confirm the age of the universe and define its radius and its mass with a good approximation.
Overview
The Karlsson Peaks in the Quasar's Redshift Distribution as an Indication for Circling Light in a Non-Expanding Universe is a five-page paper by Thierry De Mees , released in June 2009 and catalogued here under 2008 in the General Science Journal .
It takes up a long-standing claim in the dissident cosmology literature: that quasar redshifts are not smoothly distributed but cluster at preferred values. K. G. Karlsson identified peaks at z = 0.06, 0.30, 0.60, 0.96, 1.41 and 1.96, with further peaks at 2.63 and 3.46 predicted, and found them evenly spaced in log(1+ z ) at intervals of 0.089.
De Mees's starting point is not expansion but tired light. filename: The Mediums for Light are Hiding in Plain Sight.html
title: The Mediums for Light are Hiding in Plain Sight
content_preview:
Title The Mediums for Light are Hiding in Plain Sight
Author(s) Richard O Calkins
Keywords propagation of light
Published 2015
No. of pages 12
Abstract
The propagation of light remains one of the enduring mysteries of science. Unlike every other known kind of wave, it travels at a constant speed without a medium of propagation. What supports its travel in empty space? Why is its speed so constant? And why is it so very fast? Even Einstein gave up trying to puzzle it out and simply stated the propagation of light as a postulate. While Maxwell’s equations explain the behavior (the what) of light, they don’t explain the how. They show that the speed of light is determined by two constants - epsilon and mu - but not why these two constants have the values that they do rather than having some other values. So our questions remain: how and why? Maxwell’s equations actually do answer these questions. We just haven’t understood the message because of our human laundry list of implicit assumptions about the characteristics required of medium of propagation. As often happens with implicit assumptions, nearly all of them are wrong.
Light has not one but two mediums of propagation. The electric fields in electromagnetic waves are the medium of propagation for the magnetic fields, and the magnetic fields are the medium of propagation for the electric fields. Their dance with each other is what moves light through empty space, much like molecules of air do when propagating sound. Ironically, since the waves of light and the dancing electric and magnetic fields are the same things, the mediums of propagation quite literally have been hiding in plain sight.
This paper examines both the equation for the speed of sound and Maxwell’s equations from a new perspective. In essence, it performs a mathematical autopsy of both to illuminate what lies within and, in the process, solves the mysteries of light’s propagation as simply the laws of physics at work.

Einstein's 1915 calculation, which recovered the figure from general relativity without adjustable parameters, is generally regarded as the theory's first and cleanest empirical success.

This is not so. This is impossible except on an expanding Earth. Palaeomagnetic measurements show that all of the continents except Antarctica have converged on the Arctic by several tens of degrees since the Permian. Wholly independent data from the Triassic Jurassic and Cretaceous give the same conclusion in progressively diminishing degree. Yet throughout this time the Arctic has been an area of extension. This is absurd unless the Earth has greatly expanded. Several other independent sets of data set out herein require Earth expansion. Expansion has been denied on limits of palaeogravity, palaeomagnetic compilations, and the condition of other planets. Many of these criticisms are Quixotic ? setting up a model. then proceeding to demolish it, but the criticisms do not apply to the model herein proposed Others are simply invalid.

An object released from hand and falling to ground is such a common occurrence that it is not even perceived as a phenomenon of nature. The universality of gravitation was demonstrated in the theories of Nicholaus Copernicus, Johannes Kepler and Isaac Newton. The latter's insight of explaining the movement of celestial objects by the same force that acts near the surface of the Earth and causes the fall of bodies was an important step that greatly expanded our knowledge. Notwithstanding the huge efforts directed towards elucidating the nature of gravitation, no satisfactory results have been attained and no meaningful theory has been proposed so far. It is not quantitative evaluations or mathematical methods that are in want, but a picture that can be comprehended qualitatively in the first place. Only after such a qualitative picture has been found can it be hoped that a meaningful mathematical theory be constructed. The unerring methods of calculus would then make possible finding results whose physical interpretation would point to phenomena possible to occur, giving in the same time the conditions that are needed for them to occur. The present work endeavors to propose such a theory and shows that the gravitational force is essentially Archimedic in nature, acting on all bodies immersed in the vast ocean of aether. On the contrary, a drift of the interference fringes must be observed in order to support Einstein's relativity. The Ten Assumptions of Science: Toward a New Scientific Worldview is a 2004 book by Glenn Borchardt setting out the philosophical foundation on which his later work — neomechanics , Infinite Universe Theory , the Neomechanical Gravitation Theory and Universal Cycle Theory — is built. It is the shortest and most fundamental of his books, and the one everything else in his programme depends on.
Its argument is that science does not rest on proven absolutes but on assumptions; that every assumption has an equally unprovable opposite; and that most of the confusion in modern physics and cosmology comes from mixing deterministic and indeterministic assumptions without noticing that a choice has been made at all.
Method
Borchardt takes his criteria from the philosopher R. G. Collingwood. A genuinely fundamental assumption has two marks: it always has an opposite, and it can never be completely proven. When more than one is adopted, a third requirement applies — they must be consupponible , meaning that assuming any one of them permits assuming all the others without contradiction.
He presents the ten as satisfying that test as a set, and their indeterministic opposites as forming a rival consupponible set which is the foundation of belief in the supernatural. His claim is not that his assumptions are proven, but that they are coherent, that they are the ones science actually needs, and that the alternatives cannot be held together without contradiction. The assumption of infinity is the thread running through all ten.

The Theory of Gravitation (2007) is a book by the Romanian researcher Sorin Cezar Cosofret , published at Iaşi by Editura Elkadot. It sets out what he calls the theory of planetary vortexes — an account in which the solar system is not a set of bodies moving through empty space under mutual attraction, but a set of bodies moving through a real, moving interplanetary medium which acts on them.
Its most unusual feature is its modesty about what it is attacking. Cosofret states at the outset that the theory is:
not intended as a negation of the Newton's theory of gravitation, but as its complement.
— Sorin Cezar Cosofret, The Theory of Gravitation
The proposal
The argument begins with an observation about what Newtonian celestial mechanics assumes. It:
describes the movement of celestial bodies which constitutes the solar system (planets, comets, asteroids) as in a vacuum, in a completely void, matter less space.
— Sorin Cezar Cosofret, The Theory of Gravitation
That idealisation was reasonable in 1687 and is now known to be false in detail: the space between the planets contains solar wind, dust, plasma and field. Cosofret's move is to ask what follows if that medium is not merely present but in global motion — a vortex.
The consequence is that a planet is subject to two interactions rather than one: the familiar Sun–planet attraction, and an additional interaction between the interplanetary environment and the body moving through it . The second appears in the equations as a corrective term.
The nature of the corrective term
The character of that term is the theory's most carefully stated point, and it is easy to misread. Cosofret specifies that the correction:
refers to the nature (density) of the celestial body, and we may not apply this corrective term to a fundamental interaction.
— Sorin Cezar Cosofret, The Theory of Gravitation

Abstract
The exact mechanism of the Unity principle and the basic constituent of the physical Universe are disclosed with their consequences for theoretical physics. It is shown briefly how the Universe works at its micro and macro levels.
Overview
Peter Kohut's paper sets out a single-element ontology for physics. Everything that exists — matter, energy, space, the vacuum , and every force field — is claimed to be built from one entity, the quantum dipole : an indivisible bipolar connection between a "+" pole and a "−" pole, in permanent oscillation through their mutual attraction and repulsion. Every positive pole is directly connected to every negative pole in the universe, so that the familiar philosophical slogan "everything is connected with everything else" is given, in Kohut's words, an "exact mechanism". Space is not a container in which dipoles sit; each dipole is a quantum of space, and the volume of the universe is simply the number of dipoles it contains.
The paper's departure from the mainstream account is total rather than local. The basics of modern physics namely the Victorian theory of Everything - keeps getting ignored in physics discussions. Einstein was working from it, so why is it ignored?
Summary
Roger J Anderton hosted this one himself, and it was aimed less at the mainstream than at his own society. His complaint: if relativity is wrong, there was already a unified theory of everything in place before it, and neither the mainstream nor the dissidents show any interest in going back to it. A hundred people agree Einstein is wrong and produce a hundred private theories instead.
Einstein's point particles
The first half rested on a translation. The commonly used English version of the 1905 paper reads: "Let there be in motion in an electromagnetic field an electrically charged particle (in the sequel called an electron)". Arthur I Miller's translation gives "a point particle possessing electric charge". Anderton put the German passage up and showed that the word rendered simply as "particle" is punktförmiges — point-shaped — so the standard translation drops it.
His inference is that special relativity is a point-particle theory, which he thinks comes as a surprise to many, and that the point-particle tradition runs from Euclid's geometry through Boscovich — and Kant with him — to Einstein. Modern physics is built on it. That, he argued, is why it is no use inventing an alternative mathematics with no connection to Euclidean geometry: the geometry, minus the fifth postulate, is the mathematics classical physics is actually made of, and it gets harder as it develops rather than simpler.

Ratcliffe's starting point is not a particular observation but a structural complaint, and he states it in the book's own words:
In the course of using essential theories of science in my decades-long attempt to demystify the heavens, I became increasingly frustrated by ideas that just didn't harmonise. If we were uncovering the truth, I reasoned, then the component parts devised by disparate specialists should dovetail neatly together. But they don't. Classical Newtonian mechanics doesn't see eye-to-eye with Einstein's relativity; both are sneered at by quantum mechanics. Theories highly successful in their own right seemed when compared with one another to be describing different universes.
— Hilton Ratcliffe, The Virtue of Heresy

That was a train-smash, both for me and for the progress of science, as I understood it. This book is an account of that crisis.

Abstract
Forces acting on particles in a thermodynamic system may be diffusive, electric, electromagnetic or gravitationaL It is shown here that, regardless of their nature, such forces can either be motive, or dissipative. Near equilibrium, dissipative forces are locally proportional to the particle flux densities, and lead to Ohm's law, Flick's law, and other dispositive laws, and the Einstein diffusion-mobility/viscosity relation. But particle flux densities are locally indeterminate from motive forces. The interaction of all motive and dispositive forces is governed by a fundamental global relation: the law of conservation of energy, as applied to the entire system. This interaction of all motive and dispositive forces in a system is expressed sufficiently close to equilibrium. It will be shown that at equilibrium, each identifiable, dispositive force, and its corresponding particle flux vanish, and each identifiable motive field, likewise, falls into a state of self-balancing. For, each such force becomes conservative, and the work it does per particle vanishes around every possible closed loop in the system, and, consequently, cannot drive any particle flux. In effect, therefore, at equilibrium, not only the balancing occurs for each constituent, as is the case in classical thermodynamics, but also by each identifiable process. This basic result has interesting ramifications concerning the possible explanation of some mysterious interfacial phenomena to be cited.

Almost every Tesla source collected on this wiki passes through that episode, and it cannot be read without knowing what Edison actually did and did not do. The second is the Edison effect : in the course of the lamp work Edison observed a current crossing a vacuum, patented it, and set it aside without explanation, leaving the discovery to become the vacuum tube in other hands. Three Wise Men is a thirteen-page illustrated dialogue in which Salvatore E Iaquinta stages an argument between Albert Einstein, "Isaac" ( Isaac Newton ) and Galileo about the light-clock thought experiment. Iaquinta argues that a light pulse, once it has been emitted , carries no component of the source's velocity, because it did not exist until the moment of emission. In a vehicle moving at v with a laser on the ceiling aimed at a target on the floor, the pulse should therefore travel straight down in the ground frame and diagonally in the vehicle frame — the exact reverse of the standard picture — and should miss the target by an amount proportional to v / c . The Three-Dimensional Spiral String Theory ( 3D-SST ) is a unified theory of matter, radiation and spacetime developed by the Russian-American engineer and independent theorist Vladimir B Ginzburg from 1993 onward. It holds that everything in nature — particles, fields, radiation, and the aether itself — is built from a single spiral spacetime element called the toryx and its offspring the helyx . Present explanations on mechanism of tides are based either on centrifugal action or on gravitational attraction. Centrifugal force (due to motion of a body in circular path), used in analytical solutions, is an imaginary effort. Explanations, based on actions by an imaginary effort, cannot be factually correct. One of the fundamental assumptions used to derive the equation for gravitational attraction is that whole matter content (mass) of each body is concentrated at its center. This makes it illogical to assume that different parts of same body have different magnitudes of gravitational attraction towards another body. Therefore, explanations on tides, based on differences in gravitational attractions on different parts of bodies, are perversions of present theory on gravitational attraction. Apparent orbital motion of a body about epicenter of a system is also used in some explanations. In nature, no free body can orbit around another moving body [3] in geometrically closed path. Orbital path of earth about the sun (or that of moon about earth) is not circular or elliptical around a central body but it zigzags about sun's (earth's) median path in space. Hence, an explanation based on revolution of earth around an epicenter is pure imagination. According to current rules of dynamics, more than one external linear effort on a rigid body can produce only one resultant linear motion. Yet, earth experiences distinctly separate sets of tides from central forces towards moon and sun. Only logical reason for lunar tides to be greater than solar tides is that the central force between earth and moon is greater than that between earth and sun. This cannot be substantiated by current gravitational laws.

Time out for Time Dilation and Light Quanta is a four-page paper by John-Erik Persson of Hägersten, Sweden, published in 2014. It is a survey of what he takes to be "different interpretational errors in physics", each stated compactly and referred back to his longer monograph Light Without Energy .
The opening argument concerns the swimmer analogy for the Michelson–Morley experiment. Persson holds that the transverse arm suffers no ether-wind delay at all, because the mirrors' boundary conditions fix the wavefronts parallel to themselves: "Light takes the shortest path in the frame of the ether." On this reading the √(1−β²) factor for the transverse arm is spurious, Stokes introduced it wrongly, and Einstein then invented time dilation to conceal the error.
The apparent slowing of moving clocks is instead a property of clocks. An ether wind distorts the Coulomb field in one direction only, the bound electron adapts to the distorted field, and its orbital period changes by (1−β²) −1 . There is no dilation of time itself.
The rest of the paper sorts phenomena into first- and second-order effects. First order: stellar aberration is "useless" as an ether probe since it depends on the observer's change of motion, while the Sagnac corrections in GPS and light bending near the Sun are genuine first-order signatures. Tired light is the general name for a family of proposals in which the red shift of light from distant galaxies is caused by a gradual loss of energy by photons as they travel through space, rather than by a recession of the galaxies or an expansion of space. Because a photon's energy is proportional to its frequency, any process that steadily drains energy from light over great distances would lengthen its wavelength — that is, shift it toward the red — by an amount that grows with distance, reproducing the linear redshift–distance relation (Hubble's law) within a static, non-expanding universe . In mainstream physics and astronomy tired light is regarded as an obsolete and falsified idea; on this wiki it is documented as a serious alternative to the expanding-universe interpretation that underlies the Big Bang , and a substantial body of supporting and reviving work is collected in the section below .
The basic idea
The observed fact that light from distant galaxies is shifted toward longer (redder) wavelengths in proportion to their distance is not in dispute. What is disputed is its interpretation . In the standard cosmology the redshift is read as a Doppler-like effect of galaxies receding from us as space expands. Tired-light models instead attribute the redshift to some interaction between the traveling photons and the intervening medium — or to a novel property of light propagation itself — that removes a small, fixed fraction of a photon's energy per unit distance. This presentation will discuss issues in modern cosmology. The ideas of Dark matter, Dark Energy, The Cosmic Microwave background and other topics basic to modern cosmological models will be discussed and critiqued.
Summary
Harry Ricker continued his survey of standard cosmology with the two hypotheses that carry most of its weight, and closed on a conclusion about how the field works rather than about the physics. The session ran without a separate host, with Vladimir S Netchitailo and Nick Percival taking most of the discussion; Ricker's slides did not advance on the audience's screens for the first stretch, so part of the material had to be gone over twice.
Dark matter follows from inflation
Ricker's central point is one rarely put this plainly: dark matter is not primarily an astronomical inference but a requirement of a particle-physics programme. Dark matter is what closes the gap — non-baryonic, smoothly distributed, and cold rather than hot, since hot dark matter would not let galaxies condense.

Andrija Radović's paper, published in Il Nuovo Cimento B in January 2009, takes the two-century-old puzzle of the Faraday disc — that spinning the magnet changes nothing, while spinning the disc generates a voltage — and argues that the standard reading of it is exactly backwards. Radović frames the question as a choice between two positions he labels the M hypothesis , in which physical fields have their own velocities that "mainly match the velocities of the fields' sources", and the N hypothesis , in which fields have no velocity at all and poles merely change the magnitude of eternally existing fields. Volume 3
Number 4
No. of pages 15
Pages 318-329
Abstract
It is shown that a very small change in the initial angle of orientation of a tumbling cube can be detected by a shift in the endpoint of the trajectory after the cube travels a minimum distance. Specifically, if a cube travels forward in the x direction, with s the number of forward steps (tumbles) in the trajectory, the average sideways deviation DY in final position produced by a change in initial angle 0 dq is given by DY = a(s ? s 0 ), where a is the average length of the sideways step during each tumble and s 0 a term which depends logarithmically on 0 dq . It is proposed that the reason cubes (dice) are popular in games of chance is because this ability of the cube trajectory to magnify small changes allows the possibility for mental influence to act. A general outline is given for experiments using traveling cubes which can test for the action of mental influence.
Overview
This is a mechanics paper written in the service of a parapsychological question. Jean E. Burns asks how large a macroscopic effect a very small perturbation applied at the start of a die's trajectory can produce by the time the die comes to rest, and answers with a closed-form estimate: the sideways displacement grows linearly with the number of tumbles once a threshold number of tumbles has been passed, and the threshold depends only logarithmically on the size of the initial perturbation. The point of the exercise is that an influence too small to observe directly — Burns explicitly declines to specify its magnitude, assuming only that it is small — can nonetheless be detected at the end of a long enough trajectory.
The framing acknowledges from the outset that the existence of mental influence is unsettled.

Sergiu Udrea (who publishes under the name Udrea Sergiu ) is a Romanian-born independent researcher based in Montreal, Canada. Born on 1 February 1975, he is the author of a theory in which light is a wave carried by a material aether , set out in his 2011 work New Theory of Light and Aether .
Scientific work
Udrea's starting point is the classical principle that a wave requires a medium: if light is a wave, he argues, it must propagate through something, and that something is the aether . On his account the many properties of light that are otherwise puzzling — and that the relativistic rejection of the aether leaves without a physical picture — should instead follow naturally from the properties of the aether itself.
He requires the aether not merely to carry light but also to support material particles and the interactions between light and matter, and he takes up the classical difficulty of how a transverse wave can propagate within such a medium. The work belongs to the tradition of aether theories that reject the special-relativistic account of light travelling through empty space and seek to restore a physical medium of propagation. It is not accepted by mainstream physics, which since 1905 has dispensed with the luminiferous aether.

Úlpio Nascimento is a Portuguese research engineer, retired from the Laboratório Nacional de Engenharia Civil (National Laboratory for Civil Engineering) in Lisbon. His professional field is the mechanics of deformable materials, and it shapes the physics he went on to write: both of his recorded papers treat space as an elastic medium and reason about it with the tools of continuum mechanics.
The earlier, " On the Trail of the Fresnel's Search for an Aether Wind " (1998), appeared in Apeiron and returns to the nineteenth-century optical experiments — Fresnel's drag coefficient and the searches for a motion of the Earth through the light-carrying medium.
The later and much longer work, " A Quantum Gravity Model Foregoing the Dark Matter " (2007), sets out a complete model. Space is an etherspace : a discrete elastic lattice whose units, the etherons , are electrons and positrons, frictionless among themselves. Material particles are inclusions that deform the lattice, and the elastic energy stored in that deformation is their mass, in accordance with E = mc ²; a moving particle deforms the medium further, and the increase is its kinetic energy. Because the time light takes to cross one etheron is postulated constant however deformed the etheron may be, absolute time is recovered and the Galilean transformation revalidated.
From the elasticity of this lattice Nascimento derives a gravitational force law in which Newton's constant is not constant but depends on the radii of the attracting bodies. He draws three consequences and states them plainly: heavier bodies fall marginally more slowly, gravity continues to rise rather than fall as one descends inside a body, and the rotation of galaxies follows from baryonic matter alone without dark matter. Abstract
The beginning of this author's work with rotating objects began with moment of inertia measurements of constrained gyroscopes undergoing forced precession. The increased moments of inertia discovered for precessional motion were translated into a series of measurements on pendulums with rotating bobs. Although the discovery of the inertial effects associated with precession and pendulum oscillations were highly suggestive, this author greatly resisted attempts to force him to drop a rotating object for two reasons.
Overview
Understanding the Dropping of the Spinning Ball Experiment is a five-page paper by Bruce E DePalma dated 3 May 1977. It is the sequel to Gravity & The Spinning Ball Experiment , written seven weeks earlier, and its interest lies chiefly in how far it departs from it.
DePalma recounts the sequence that led to the experiment: moment-of-inertia measurements on constrained gyroscopes in forced precession, then pendulums with rotating bobs, and only reluctantly the dropping of a free rotating object — a step he calls "a leap into the dark", since "there was no reason to expect inertial alteration to affect the rate of fall of a released object". The stroboscopic result — a spinning ball rising higher than a non-spinning control launched at the same speed, and then falling faster — "was so startling and anomalous as to have taken me 5 years to understand."
The interpretation offered here is new, and it withdraws the gravitational claim of the earlier paper: "The momentous fact is that there is no special interaction between rotation and gravity. Unified Physics is a 1988 technical report by Reginald Irvan Gray , issued by the Naval Surface Warfare Center at Dahlgren, Virginia. It is the book-length statement of the unified account of electromagnetism and gravitation that Gray, a physicist employed at the laboratory, worked on for some three decades and called electromagnetogravitism .
Its provenance is what makes it unusual. Unified-field-theory monographs of this kind are ordinarily self-published; this one was printed and distributed by a United States Navy weapons laboratory as an official technical report, and is accordingly a U.S. government document in the public domain — freely readable in full, as set out under Availability below.
Background
Gray's programme long predates the report. He set it out in 1970 in a Naval Weapons Laboratory technical note, Electromagnetogravitism (NWL Technical Note TN-T-1/70), and again about 1975 in a 65-page paper, " A New Theory of Electromagnetism and Gravity ", which closes by describing itself as "a synopsis of a book which is soon to be published."
That paper is the clearest brief statement of what the larger work sets out to do, and is worth quoting since it is Gray's own:
For over 300 years the conflict between electromagnetic wave and particle theories has engaged the minds of physicists and mathematicians, the cleavage being accentuated rather than reduced by the advent of wave mechanics. Unipolar Induction Problems was a live session presented by James Keene on 21 January 2023 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
Since the 1800s, when the first experiments were done by Faraday, phenomena reported in the 1900s suggest several alternative explanations for Faraday's results. These potential problems and experimental designs which might settle the issues involved are presented.
Summary
James Keene on possible confounds in the unipolar induction experiments, the latest of a run of sessions on the subject: three by Harry Ricker on Faraday's original experiments and the competing explanations of them, one by Bob Gray applying Weber's electrodynamics, and one by Ian J Cowan , who hosted this one, on Al Kelly 's repetitions. Keene, whose own field is particle physics and quantum mechanics rather than electromagnetism, said the previous speakers had been good enough to force him to put on his thinking cap, and offered questions rather than a conclusion.
The setup and the complaint
The apparatus he took as standard is the one from Cowan's video: a copper disc symmetric about an axis, a cylindrical bar magnet with one pole close to the disc and separated from it by a little air, brush contacts on the shaft and at the rim, and a meter. Spin the disc and a small voltage appears — typically under fifty millivolts.
His opening criticism was methodological. The experiments do not clearly exclude the competing theories — Maxwell's, Faraday's, Weber's and others — and, as far as he could recall from the earlier sessions, the experimentalists do not calculate the millivolts each theory predicts. Without predicted values there is no statistical test that could distinguish among them.

Using Instruments is a two-page article by Leslee A Kulba , published in 2010 in issue 48 of the Electric Spacecraft Journal , the journal's final double issue. It is the sixth part of the ten-part handbook on perpetual motion and its testing that Kulba, the journal's technical editor, contributed to that issue, and it is the shortest of the ten.
The text of the article has not been recoverable, and this page describes its subject and its place in the series rather than its argument.
The subject
The instrument is part of the circuit
The first thing a meter does is change what it is measuring. A voltmeter draws current through its input impedance; an ammeter inserts a resistance and drops a burden voltage across it; an oscilloscope probe adds capacitance, typically ten to twenty picofarads for a times-one probe, which is enough to load a high-impedance node and round off the edges of the very waveform being examined. A times-ten probe reduces the loading tenfold at the cost of a tenfold reduction in signal.
In a high-impedance or fast circuit these are not refinements. They are the difference between a reading and an artefact, and they are systematic — repeating the measurement will reproduce the error exactly.
Bandwidth and rise time
An instrument reports what it can follow. A meter with a 1 kHz bandwidth presented with a 20 kHz switching waveform reports something, and that something is not the peak, the average or the RMS value. For an oscilloscope the usable rule is that displayed rise time and true rise time combine in quadrature, and that the instrument's own rise time is roughly 0.35 divided by its bandwidth; a scope needs a bandwidth several times the highest frequency of interest before the displayed edge can be trusted.

Valery P. Dmitriyev is a Russian theoretical physicist based in Moscow, affiliated in his published work with Lomonosov Moscow State University. Since the early 1990s he has pursued a single programme: the construction of explicit mechanical analogies, drawn from the mechanics of continuous media, for the equations of quantum physics and electromagnetism.
Work
Dmitriyev's substratum is what the nineteenth century called the vortex sponge — an ideal fluid threaded in all directions by thin, straight vortex filaments — and his method is to identify the equations governing disturbances of that medium with the equations of physics. Three strands recur across his papers.
The elastic model of the physical vacuum. Treating the vacuum as a solid-like medium whose displacement field corresponds to the magnetic vector potential, he recovers the structure of electromagnetism from elasticity. This line was published in Mechanics of Solids in 1992 and developed in Nuovo Cimento A in 1998.
Vortex filaments and the quantum equations. A helical disturbance on a vortex filament, evolving under the local induction approximation of classical vortex dynamics, obeys an equation of Schrödinger form; adding the filament's elastic response produces a Klein–Gordon-like equation. On this reading the wave function is the position vector of a curve rather than an abstract amplitude. Mechanical Analogy for the Wave-Particle: Helix on a Vortex Filament and Mechanical Interpretation of the Klein-Gordon Equation , both published in Apeiron in 2001, set this out.
Turbulent advection and relativistic effects. In a series of papers from 1993 onwards he argues that the effects usually attributed to relativity — and the mass–energy relation in particular — can be recovered from the behaviour of discontinuities advected in a turbulent fluid, work summarised in The Substratum Origin of Relativistic Effects and E=mc2 in the Turbulent Aether

Scientific Theory
Name Variable speed of light
Type Family of theories in which c is not a universal constant
Author(s) Einstein (1911); John W. Moffat (1992); Andreas Albrecht and Jo Magueijo (1998); and many independent researchers
Keywords Light , speed of light, c , Relativity , Aether , Emission Theory , Redshift , one-way light speed, Cosmology
Year 1911 (Einstein); 1992– (modern VSL cosmology)
Variable speed of light ( VSL ) is the proposition that the speed of light c is not a universal constant — that it may differ with position, with epoch, with the gravitational potential, with the medium, with direction of travel, or with the motion of the source.
The proposition matters more than it may appear. The constancy of c is the second postulate of special relativity and the foundation on which the Lorentz transformation, time dilation, length contraction and the relativity of simultaneity all rest. If c varies, that structure requires reworking. It is for this reason that VSL is among the most frequently revisited subjects on this wiki, and also why it attracts researchers with otherwise incompatible positions.
VSL is not one theory but several. The label covers proposals that differ profoundly in what they claim, in how respectable they are considered, and in what would count as evidence for them. Distinguishing them is the first task of this article, because arguments against one variety are routinely presented as though they told against all of them.
Why the question is subtle
Two features of the problem make it harder than it looks, and both are worth stating before the varieties are set out.
The metre is defined by c . Since 1983 the metre has been defined as the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second. The speed of light in vacuum is therefore fixed by definition at exactly 299,792,458 m/s, and can no longer be measured — a measurement that appeared to show a different value would be interpreted as a change in the length of the metre, not in c

Vicente L. "Vince" Lopes is an American environmental scientist and educator who is a professor of Environmental Studies at Texas State University in San Marcos, Texas. Lopes earned his Ph.D. in hydrology and water resources science from the University of Arizona . He served as an associate professor at the University of Arizona before joining Texas State University in January 2005, where he was later promoted to full professor. He is based in San Marcos, Texas.
Work
Lopes's early research centered on watershed hydrology, with an emphasis on the mathematical and distributed modeling of water and sediment yield and catchment-scale erosion. Abstract
We derive the virial theorem for Weber's law applied to gravitation and electromagnetism.
Overview
Virial Theorem for Weber's Law is a four-page research note published in 2004, pp. 67–70. The wiki's infobox names Andre K T Assis ; the paper has three authors — R. S. Mendes and L. C. Malacarne of the Universidade Estadual de Maringá, and Assis of Unicamp, who completed the work under an Alexander von Humboldt fellowship.
Weber's 1846 force law makes the interaction between two particles depend not only on their separation but on the rate at which that separation changes. The interaction energy is
U ij = (k ij /r ij )(1 − ξ ṛ ij ²/2c²)
with k ij = −Gm i m j and ξ = 6 for gravitation, or k ij = q i q j /4πε 0 and ξ = 1 for electromagnetism. The corresponding force carries a term in r̈ as well as ṛ², so the force on a particle depends on its own acceleration.
The authors note that treatments of Weber's law had been confined to one or two bodies, and set out to begin a statistical treatment of the many-body case. They take the standard virial construction — dot Newton's second law with r i , sum over particles, time-average, and use ⟨dA/dt⟩ = 0 for bounded or periodic motion — and apply it to the Weber force.
The result is
⟨U⟩ = −2⟨T⟩
identical in form to the Newtonian virial theorem, with U now Weber's velocity-dependent potential. They close by suggesting applications to plasma physics and to "the formation or stability of the solar system or of galaxies", describing the note as "a first step in this direction".

The derivation is correct

(k/r)[1 + (ξ/c²)(r r̈ − ṛ²/2)]

Abstract
The concept of free will is central to our lives, as we make day-to-day decisions, and to our culture, in our ethical and legal systems. The very concept implies that what we choose can produce a change in our physical environment, whether by pressing a switch to turn out electric lights or choosing a long-term plan of action which can affect many people. Yet volition is not a part of presently known physical laws, and it is not even known whether it exists -- no physics experiments have ever established its presence. (We will use the terms volition and free will synonymously in this article.) The purpose of this article is to make two points: first, that free will cannot be accounted for by presently known physical laws, and second, that if free will exists, any description of its effects in the physical world necessarily would constitute a radical addition to presently known physical laws...
Overview
Jean E. Burns, a consciousness researcher writing in the Journal of Consciousness Studies , sets out to establish two propositions and to survey the consequences of holding both. The first is that free will cannot be accounted for by physics as it now stands, since present laws "encompass only determinism and quantum randomness, and neither of these are what is meant by free will." The second is the sharper one: if free will does exist, then any statement of how it produces effects in the physical world would itself be a radical addition to physical law — not a philosophical thesis about the mind, but new physics.

Wallace Kantor (born 1922) is an American experimental physicist, based in San Diego, California, known for a long series of experiments and theoretical papers challenging Einstein's special theory of relativity . He is best remembered for his 1962 claim to have measured a dependence of the speed of light on the motion of its source — a result that would support an emission (ballistic) theory of light against the second postulate of special relativity.
Scientific work
The 1962 moving-source experiment
Kantor's most-cited result is the experiment reported in "Direct First-Order Experiment on the Propagation of Light from a Moving Source" ( Journal of the Optical Society of America , 1962). Using glass plates mounted on a rotating arm between the mirrors of a modified Michelson–Morley interferometer, he reported a first-order fringe shift — on the order of the roughly 2.9 fringes predicted by emission theory — which he interpreted as showing that light passing through the moving glass is re-emitted at speed c relative to the glass rather than to any fixed frame. If correct, the result would contradict the constancy of the speed of light.
The claim was tested and not confirmed. In 1964 H. E. Babcock and T. G. Bergman repeated the experiment with roughly four times the sensitivity and, where Kantor's emission theory predicted several fringes, found a shift of less than 0.02 fringe — a null result consistent with special relativity. Kantor's positive result is accordingly regarded by mainstream physics as an experimental artifact, though it remains a reference point in the emission-theory and critical-relativity literature.

Recent data indicate that the law of action between electric current elements proposed by Ampere is notably superior to the Lorentz (Biot-Savart) law in its ability to describe laboratory observations of currents flowing in single circuits. Ampere's law conforms to Newton's third law and thus cannot be covariantly expressed. The virtues of this approach are (a) mathematical simplicity, (b) rigorous conformity to Newton's third law, and (c) agreement with Ampere's law of action between current elements — hence with the observations just mentioned. Two different "modernizations" of Weber's approach are examined, dependent on whether energy or force methods are viewed as more fundamental in mechanics. Implications for plasma physics are touched upon.

Abstract
The Lorentz force has nothing, either mathematically or physically, to do with Maxwell's field equa-tions. Properly written F L = q( E (1) + v x B (2) ), the Lorentz force is just a phenomenological expression allowing one to describe (parametrically) the motion of a charged particle in the external fields E (1) and B (2) originating from independent sources belonging to different, decoupled systems. Electrodynamics can be built starting from a force-law between moving charges, without separately postulating field equations. There is no need for a "special" relativity theory.
